bahdanau>transformer.lead: Bahdanau attention was a patch on a recurrent decoder: a way to let it look back at encoder states instead of squeezing a sentence through one fixed vector. The Transformer kept the patch and threw away the thing it was patching.

blocks.b:
The 2014 seq2seq encoder compressed a whole source sentence into one final hidden state, and translation quality fell away sharply as sentences got longer — the vector was a bottleneck with a fixed budget. Bahdanau et al. let the decoder compute, at each output step, a weighted sum over **all** encoder states:

$$c_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} h_j, \qquad \alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp(e_{ij})}{\sum_k \exp(e_{ik})}$$

with $e_{ij} = a(s_{i-1}, h_j)$ a small feed-forward network scoring how well output position $i$ matches input position $j$. The alignment is learned jointly with translation rather than supplied, and the resulting $\alpha$ matrix turned out to be legible as a soft word alignment.

The decisive property is that $c_i$ reaches $h_j$ in **one step, for any $j$**. Distance in the sequence stopped costing accuracy.

In Bahdanau's model attention is an auxiliary channel; the recurrence is still what carries state, and it is still sequential. Vaswani et al. observed that if a one-step path between arbitrary positions is what makes attention valuable, then recurrence is contributing mainly its cost — an unparallelisable loop over sequence length.

Three changes make the removal work. Attention is applied **within** each sequence and not only across the two (self-attention), so a representation can be built without any recurrent state. The additive score $a(s,h)$ becomes a **scaled dot product**, which is a matrix multiplication and therefore fast on the hardware that was becoming available:

$$e_{ij} = \frac{q_i \cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}$$

And because attention alone is order-blind, positional encodings replace the ordering that recurrence used to supply for free.

Training time on WMT14 English–German fell from weeks to around twelve hours on eight GPUs, at higher BLEU. That is the visible result; the structural one matters more. An architecture whose cost is dense matrix multiplication rather than a sequential loop scales with accelerators, and scaling with accelerators is the precondition for everything downstream — GPT, BERT, and the observation that loss falls predictably with compute.

The bill came due in the complexity: attending over all pairs is $O(n^2)$, where the recurrent model was $O(n)$ in sequence length. For 2017 sentence lengths that was a bargain. At 100k-token contexts it is the central problem, and a decade of efficient-attention work descends from it.

transformer>gpt1.lead: GPT-1 kept the Transformer's decoder, discarded its encoder, and changed what the model was for: not translating a given sentence, but predicting the next token over any text at all — which turns the whole internet into a supervised dataset.

blocks.b:
The original Transformer is an encoder–decoder built for translation: the encoder reads the source with bidirectional self-attention, the decoder generates the target while cross-attending into it. Remove the source and the encoder has nothing to read, so GPT-1 keeps only the decoder stack — twelve layers, masked self-attention, no cross-attention.

The mask is the load-bearing part. Position $i$ may attend to $j \le i$ and no further, implemented by setting the disallowed scores to $-\infty$ before the softmax. That constraint makes the model a valid autoregressive factorisation of the joint distribution:

$$P(x) = \prod_{i} P(x_i \mid x_1,\dots,x_{i-1})$$

so every position in a sequence supplies a training signal at once, while still describing one coherent distribution over text.

The move GPT-1 is remembered for is not architectural. It trains on BooksCorpus with the plain likelihood objective

$$L_1(\mathcal{U}) = \sum_i \log P(u_i \mid u_{i-k},\dots,u_{i-1}; \Theta)$$

and then fine-tunes the same weights on each downstream task, feeding structured inputs as delimited token sequences rather than building a task-specific architecture. Task heads shrink to a linear layer.

Before this, NLP transfer mostly meant transferring **word vectors** — word2vec, GloVe — and learning the contextual machinery per task. GPT-1 transferred the machinery. It improved the state of the art on nine of twelve benchmarks, and reported that the pre-trained model already did non-trivially on some tasks with no fine-tuning at all: the observation GPT-2 and GPT-3 pushed on.

BERT, months later, made the opposite call: keep the encoder, attend in both directions, and train by masking tokens instead of predicting the next one. Bidirectional context is strictly more informative for **understanding** a fixed input, and BERT duly overtook GPT-1 on classification and span-extraction benchmarks.

What the causal mask preserves is the ability to **generate**, and a training signal at every position rather than at the ~15% that are masked. Which mattered more was not settled by argument but by scale: the autoregressive objective kept improving as models and corpora grew, and the line from here runs through GPT-2 and GPT-3 to the instruction-followed models.

gpt3>flamingo.lead: What crossed from GPT-3 to Flamingo was not weights but a claim about interfaces: that a sufficiently large language model is programmed by its context, and that the context need not be text. Flamingo took a frozen language model as a fixed substrate and spent its entire design budget on getting images into that context without disturbing it.

blocks.b:
GPT-3's result was that a task could be specified by putting a few worked examples in the prompt, with no gradient step and no per-task head. Two consequences mattered downstream. The first is that the capability lives in weights worth leaving alone: fine-tuning a general model on a narrow downstream set buys that set and spends the generality. The second is that the context window is an undifferentiated conditioning slot — the model does not know or care what produced the vectors it attends over, only that they are in the sequence.

That second property is what makes a cross-modal move thinkable at all. If conditioning is just tokens in a sequence, then a picture that can be turned into something token-shaped inherits the whole in-context machinery for free, including the few-shot behaviour that nobody knows how to train directly.

blocks.h: What Flamingo added to keep it
blocks.b: Flamingo froze a Chinchilla language model completely, and froze the vision encoder too. What it threw away was joint multimodal pretraining from scratch. What it had to add was three things that make freezing survivable. A **Perceiver Resampler** maps a variable number of visual features — one image, many, video frames — onto a fixed small set of latent tokens, so cost does not grow with resolution or frame count. **Gated cross-attention layers** are interleaved between the frozen language blocks, with the branch output scaled by $\tanh(\alpha)$ and $\alpha$ initialised at zero, so at the first step the network computes exactly the original language model and the visual pathway is learned as a departure from it rather than a perturbation of it. And an attention mask lets each text token see only the most recent preceding image, which is what makes interleaved image–text web pages trainable and lets the model accept more images at test time than it ever saw in training.

blocks.h: What it changed, and the bill
blocks.b:
Multimodal few-shot became something you do by writing a prompt. On a number of the captioning and visual question-answering benchmarks Flamingo reported, prompting with a few dozen examples matched or beat systems fine-tuned on those datasets, with no gradient update at all. More durably, frozen-backbone-plus-adapter became the default vision-language recipe: BLIP-2's query transformer and the projection-layer models that followed are the same bet with different couplings.

The cost is that everything the language model is wrong about is inherited unchanged. Nothing in the training signal can correct a language prior, so confident ungrounded assertion, weak counting and poor reading of text in images all survive intact — the visual pathway can only argue with the prior, not rewrite it. And the interleaved web corpus that makes the recipe work was never released, which made the reproduction problem a data problem rather than an architectural one.

transformer>whisper.lead: Whisper is the least architecturally interesting speech model of its generation, and that is deliberate. It uses an encoder–decoder Transformer close enough to the 2017 original to be uninteresting, so that whatever the system does well is attributable to 680,000 hours of weakly supervised web audio rather than to a modelling trick.

blocks.b:
The Transformer's contribution to speech was not any speech-specific mechanism but the demonstration that a sequence-to-sequence model with cross-attention learns its own alignment. Recognition had spent decades on explicit alignment machinery: hidden Markov state alignment, then CTC marginalising over monotonic alignments, with separate acoustic, pronunciation and language models fused at decode time. Attention makes the correspondence between a continuous input sequence and a discrete output sequence a by-product of training rather than a component to be designed.

By 2022 the second thing the architecture supplied was predictability. Its response to more parameters and more data was well enough characterised that a pure data-scaling experiment was a sound experiment to run — you could attribute the outcome to the corpus, because the architecture was a known quantity.

The model takes an 80-channel log-mel spectrogram over a fixed 30-second window, passes it through two convolutions whose second has a stride of two, and then runs an ordinary encoder–decoder stack. Thrown away: CTC, external language-model fusion, per-dataset fine-tuning, and — the consequential one — clean human transcripts, replaced by whatever the web had.

Two additions make that work. The decoder's own vocabulary carries a **task protocol**: special tokens for the language, for transcribe versus translate, for whether timestamps are wanted, for no speech at all. One autoregressive decoder therefore does what a pipeline of separate systems used to. And the corpus was filtered hard to remove machine-generated transcripts, on the reasoning that a model trained on another recogniser's output learns that recogniser's error distribution rather than the relationship between audio and words.

Supervised models trained on LibriSpeech beat Whisper on LibriSpeech and degrade badly when the recording changes; Whisper, evaluated zero-shot, makes far fewer errors than those models across accent, noise and domain shift. That reframed how recognition is assessed — the interesting number became performance off the training distribution — and made a single checkpoint the default for transcription rather than one trained per deployment.

The costs follow from the design. Every clip is padded to the same 30-second window, so the quadratic attention cost is paid in full on a two-second utterance, and long recordings must be stitched from windows, which is where timestamp drift comes from. Worse, an autoregressive decoder carries a language-model prior over what text looks like, so on silence or noise it will emit fluent, plausible, entirely invented sentences — a failure mode a CTC system structurally cannot have.

transformer>roformer.lead: Attention is permutation-invariant, so the Transformer had to inject order from outside, and its answer — add a fixed sinusoidal vector to the input embedding — was argued for only briefly and largely on convenience. RoPE replaces that addition with a rotation, which makes the attention logit a function of the offset between two tokens rather than of their two absolute indices.

blocks.b:
In the 2017 design, position enters once, at the bottom, by summation into the content embedding. Three problems follow. Position and content share one vector space and compete for its capacity. Every layer above inherits whatever of the signal survived, with no way to reintroduce it. And the logit $q_m^\top k_n$ has no enforced dependence on $m-n$: sinusoids make a relative relation expressible, since a shift is a linear map on them, but nothing requires the learned projections to use it that way. Empirically a model trained at one context length simply does not work at four times that length.

Shaw and colleagues, and later T5, answered by adding a learned relative bias directly to the logit. That works, but it introduces extra terms and parameters at every layer and destroys the property that the logit is a plain inner product — which kernelised and linear-attention approximations depend on.

RoPE keeps the injection at the level of queries and keys, and abandons additivity. Split each head's dimension into two-dimensional pairs and rotate pair $i$ of the vector at position $m$ by angle $m\theta_i$, with $\theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d}$. Because rotations compose and are orthogonal, $R_m^\top R_n = R_{n-m}$, and so

$\langle R_m q_m, R_n k_n \rangle = q_m^\top R_{n-m} k_n$

depends on the two contents and on the offset alone. The absolute indices cancel. Nothing is added to the parameter count, the logit remains an inner product, and because the rotation is applied to $q$ and $k$ inside every attention layer, positional information cannot be diluted on the way up the stack. Relative position stops being a module and becomes a property of the coordinate system.

blocks.h: Universal, for a reason it did not claim
blocks.b:
RoPE is now close to universal — PaLM, GPT-NeoX, LLaMA and most open models since apply it. The motivation that gave it its name did not survive contact with practice: a RoPE model evaluated beyond its training length degrades sharply as well, because the slowest-rotating pairs never complete a period within the trained range and beyond it are presented with angles they never saw, so the attention pattern falls apart rather than extending smoothly.

What the field did instead was edit $\theta$ after the fact. Position interpolation rescales indices back into the trained range; frequency-scaling schemes stretch the low frequencies while leaving the high ones alone; and long-context training runs simply raise the base from 10,000 to a far larger value. That is the actual legacy. Because position lives in one hyperparameter rather than in learned weights, extending context became a rescaling problem with a short fine-tune attached, not a retraining of a positional module.

dpo>grpo.lead: DPO and GRPO are both subtractions from the PPO-based RLHF stack, but they remove different pieces and answer to different bottlenecks. DPO deletes the reward model, and with it online sampling; GRPO keeps sampling and rewards and deletes the value network, replacing its baseline with the mean reward over a group of answers to the same prompt.

blocks.b:
DPO's argument is that the KL-constrained RL objective has a closed-form optimum, and that substituting that optimum into a Bradley–Terry preference likelihood turns policy optimisation into a classification loss on pairs. The reward becomes implicit, read off the policy itself as $\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}$. No reward model, no rollouts, no critic: alignment becomes an ordinary supervised training job.

The reframing mattered more than the method. It showed the reward model was a reparameterisation rather than load-bearing machinery, and that much of PPO's apparatus existed to service it. What DPO gave up is that the gradient only ever sees a fixed set of pairs; nothing the policy generates during training is evaluated. The known symptom is that the loss can be reduced by pushing the rejected response's likelihood down faster than the chosen one's, so the chosen response's probability falls too.

GRPO restores on-policy sampling and interrogates the critic instead. PPO's value network is roughly the size of the policy, must be trained alongside it, and is hard to fit on language tasks where reward arrives only at the end of a sequence. Its job is narrow: supply a baseline that reduces gradient variance. GRPO samples $G$ completions for a prompt, scores them, and lets the group be its own baseline:

$$\hat{A}_i = \frac{r_i - \mathrm{mean}(r_1, \dots, r_G)}{\mathrm{std}(r_1, \dots, r_G)}$$

with that single advantage applied to every token of completion $i$. Memory for a second large network is traded for generation: $G$ samples per prompt per optimiser step. Unlike DPO, the signal is computed on what the current policy actually produces, so exploration is back.

blocks.h: Split by what scores the answer
blocks.b:
The two now coexist by role rather than one succeeding the other, and what separates them is the cost of a reward. DPO stayed where the judgment is human preference and sampling is expensive to score — a cheap, stable post-training pass. GRPO took over where the reward is checkable: a maths answer that matches, a unit test that passes. There the scorer is free, so paying for $G$ rollouts is rational, and on-policy search is precisely what long chain-of-thought reasoning needs in order to be discovered rather than imitated. The reasoning-model wave was trained this way.

The costs are specific. Generation dominates the step time. The group baseline collapses when all $G$ samples receive the same reward, so prompts that are too easy or too hard contribute no gradient at all — later variants resample those prompts and drop the standard-deviation term, because dividing by a near-zero group standard deviation quietly inflates the update on exactly those low-variance prompts. And a verifier is still a proxy: reward hacking moves from the reward model to the checker.

elmo>bert.lead: ELMo established that a word's representation should depend on the sentence it sits in, and produced one by running two language models in opposite directions and gluing their states together. BERT took the goal and rejected the construction: in ELMo the glue is the only place the two directions ever meet.

blocks.b:
Standard practice before ELMo gave a word one vector regardless of context, so every sense of "bank" shared a point in space; earlier context-dependent schemes existed — CoVe's translation encoder, TagLM's biLM features — but none had displaced static embeddings. Peters et al. trained a two-layer biLSTM language model, maximising a forward and a backward log-likelihood that share only their token embeddings and softmax, and then, rather than taking the top layer, let each downstream task learn a scalar mixture over all of them:

$\mathrm{ELMo}_k = \gamma \sum_j s_j\, h_{k,j}$

with $h_{k,j}$ the state at token $k$ in layer $j$ and $s$ a softmax-normalised weight fitted per task. Two results carried. Contextual vectors improved every task tried — question answering, entailment, semantic role labelling, coreference, named entities, sentiment — and different depths were useful for different things, lower layers for syntax and upper layers for word sense. The vectors were frozen features, concatenated into whatever task architecture already existed.

The two directions in ELMo are trained independently and joined after the fact, so no layer of either model ever conditions on both sides at once. Devlin et al. wanted every layer to, and the obstacle is the objective rather than the engineering: under a next-token loss in a deep bidirectional network, a token can see itself through the layers below and prediction collapses into copying. **Masking is what lets the objective survive bidirectionality.** BERT corrupts roughly 15% of positions and recovers the originals from unrestricted attention over the rest; of those positions 80% become `[MASK]`, 10% a random token and 10% are left untouched, so the encoder cannot treat a masked slot as reliably marked. The recurrence goes, the frozen-feature interface goes — the whole encoder is fine-tuned behind a single linear head — and the per-task layer mixture goes with it, since the task now tunes the layers themselves.

blocks.h: What the swap bought and cost
blocks.b: Fine-tuning one pretrained encoder replaced the bespoke task architectures that ELMo still fed into, and the effect was general rather than task-specific: sentence classification, sentence-pair inference and span extraction all reduced to the same stack plus an output layer. The costs are real. Only the corrupted positions produce a training signal, so BERT extracts far less gradient per token than a left-to-right model that predicts every position, and needs more compute to compensate. The `[MASK]` symbol appears throughout pretraining and never at fine-tuning time; the 80/10/10 split softens the discrepancy without removing it. Masked positions are predicted independently given the context, so the joint distribution over several gaps is never modelled — the opening XLNet's permutation objective was built into. And a model trained to fill holes cannot emit text left to right, which is why the branch that eventually scaled was GPT's.

BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers

transformer>bert.lead: BERT is the Transformer's encoder, kept close to as written, with the decoder deleted and the causal mask deleted along with it. What travelled was a stack of layers; what made the stack worth having was the discovery that it could be pretrained once and reused everywhere.

blocks.b:
Vaswani et al. built the encoder as the half that reads, and it was bidirectional from the start: every position attends to every other in a single step, in both directions, with no mask, through multi-head attention and a position-wise feed-forward network wrapped in residual connections and layer normalisation. The decoder was the constrained half. Its self-attention adds a mask $M$ with $M_{ij} = -\infty$ for $j > i$,

$\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\right)V$

so that position $i$ cannot see the future it is being trained to predict. That mask exists solely to keep the autoregressive factorisation honest under teacher forcing. Nothing about representing a sentence requires it — it is the price of generating one, and BERT does not intend to generate.

BERT sets $M = 0$, keeps the reading half, and discards cross-attention and the decoder entirely. What had to be added is a reason for an encoder to exist with nothing attached to it: a self-supervised objective, masked-token recovery alongside next-sentence prediction, and an input format that lets one stack serve sentence pairs as well as single sentences. That means a `[CLS]` position whose final state stands for the whole sequence, `[SEP]` separators, and learned segment embeddings marking which half a token belongs to. Sinusoidal positions become learned ones, the activation becomes GELU, and the stack grows well past the translation model: twelve layers at 768 dimensions in the base configuration and twenty-four at 1024 in the large one, against the original six layers at 512.

Fine-tuning BERT behind one added linear layer beat purpose-built architectures across sentence classification, inference and span extraction, and for roughly three years the default baseline in an NLP paper was a pretrained encoder. The cost of taking the encoder alone appears in two places. Quadratic attention over learned absolute positions imposed a hard ceiling of 512 tokens, and nothing in the model extrapolates beyond the position table it was trained with, so long documents had to be chunked and stitched. More consequentially, an encoder-only model has no mechanism for emitting text, so summarisation, translation and dialogue stayed outside the family, and every new task still needed labelled data and a fine-tuning run. Both limits pushed the field back towards the decoder that BERT had thrown away.

BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers

transformer>t5.lead: Where BERT took the encoder and GPT took the decoder, T5 and BART kept both halves and asked what the intact architecture was for. The answer was that if every task is written as a string in and a string out, the original translation model already has the right shape and only needs an objective that does not require parallel data.

blocks.b: The 2017 architecture is asymmetric deliberately: an unmasked encoder that reads a whole source at once, a causally masked decoder that emits one token at a time, and cross-attention through which the decoder queries encoder states at every layer. For translation this is obviously correct, and nothing in it is specific to translation — it is the general shape of any conditional sequence problem where the input is a distinct object to be read and the output has to be constructed. What it lacked was any reason to pretrain, because translation supplies its own supervision from parallel corpora. It also carried absolute sinusoidal positions, which hand the model a coordinate system it must learn to interpret rather than a notion of relative distance it can use directly.

T5's objective is span corruption: contiguous runs of tokens are replaced in the encoder input by numbered sentinels and the decoder emits the missing spans in sequence, which makes the target far shorter than the input and so cheaper than per-token masking. BART is the same instinct with a wider menu of corruptions, of which text infilling and sentence permutation worked best. Every downstream task then becomes a string — a prefix names it, the decoder writes the answer, including answers that are not natural language, such as a similarity score spelled out as digits. The substantive architectural change is positional: T5 drops sinusoids for a learned scalar added to each attention logit, bucketed by relative offset,

$e_{ij} = \frac{q_i \cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}} + b_{f(i-j)}$

where $f$ maps the distance $i-j$ into one of a fixed set of buckets, coarser as distance grows.

The text-to-text framing outlived the model. Once inputs and outputs are both strings, a task is specified by writing it down rather than by attaching a head, and that is what prompting and instruction tuning inherit. The relative-position bias — itself a scalar simplification of Shaw et al.'s relative position representations — is what ALiBi's distance penalty descends from, one branch of a wider move away from absolute positions that also produced rotary embeddings. The accompanying study is arguably worth more than the checkpoint: a systematic sweep of objectives, corpora and architectural variants at matched budget, with the C4 corpus released alongside it. The costs are structural. An encoder-decoder spends parameters on two stacks plus a cross-attention path, which is more awkward to scale than a single stack, and the prefix format still presumes someone has assembled labelled multitask data. GPT-3 argued both away within a year, and decoder-only became the default; encoder-decoders survive where the input genuinely is a separate document to be read.

gpt1>gpt2.lead: GPT-1 established that a decoder-only language model could be pretrained once and adapted to anything, but adaptation meant a fresh output head and a supervised run for every task. GPT-2 kept the pretraining, deleted the adaptation stage, and asked the model to infer from the text what task it was being given.

blocks.b: Radford et al. trained a twelve-layer masked-self-attention decoder on a corpus of books with a plain next-token objective, then fine-tuned it discriminatively on each target task. The result that mattered was not the benchmark table but the interface. Entailment, similarity and multiple choice were rewritten as single contiguous token sequences with delimiters, so one architecture and one linear output layer covered all of them and nothing task-specific entered the network itself. Two further observations pointed forward: keeping the language-modelling loss as an auxiliary term during fine-tuning helped, and zero-shot performance on several tasks rose steadily over the course of pretraining, before any supervised signal was applied. The generative model was acquiring task behaviour as a by-product of predicting text.

Structurally GPT-2 changes little: layer normalisation moves to the input of each sub-block with a final norm added at the end, residual weights are scaled by $1/\sqrt{N}$ at initialisation for $N$ layers, context doubles to 1024 and the byte-level BPE vocabulary grows to 50257. The argument is what changes. If a task can be described in text, a sufficiently varied corpus already contains demonstrations of it, so the model should be understood as estimating

$p(\mathrm{output} \mid \mathrm{input}, \mathrm{task})$

with the task conditioned on through the same token stream as everything else. The corpus is the mechanism rather than an incidental detail: WebText was scraped from outbound Reddit links carrying at least three karma, assembled to be varied and lightly filtered. Fine-tuning and its labelled data are removed, and four sizes up to 1.5B parameters are trained to see what capacity alone buys.

Zero-shot, GPT-2 improved the state of the art on seven of the eight language-modelling datasets it was measured on, without seeing their training splits. On tasks people actually wanted done it was not competitive — summarisation and translation elicited by prompting sat far below purpose-built supervised systems, and the paper says so plainly. The load-bearing observation is the trend: every metric improved with model size, monotonically, with no sign of saturating at 1.5B. That converts an architectural question into an economic one and leads directly to scaling laws and to GPT-3. Two costs arrived with it. Evaluating a model whose corpus is a web crawl made test-set contamination a permanent methodological problem rather than an occasional one, and the staged release of weights established a precedent the field is still arguing about.

refs.t: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training (GPT-1)
Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners (GPT-2)

gpt2>gpt3.lead: GPT-2 showed that zero-shot performance improved smoothly with model size and gave no sign of levelling off. GPT-3 is the experiment of taking that curve at its word: the same architecture, roughly a hundred times the parameters, and the finding that at that scale examples placed in the prompt begin to function like training data.

blocks.b:
Four sizes, one corpus, one objective and a monotone improvement in zero-shot metrics from 117M to 1.5B — that is what GPT-2 supplied, and it is a claim about extrapolation rather than about any particular task. Kaplan et al. then made it quantitative: cross-entropy loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute across several orders of magnitude,

$L(N) \approx \left(\frac{N_c}{N}\right)^{\alpha_N}$

with $N$ the non-embedding parameter count, and with exponents stable enough to predict a model's loss before it is trained. That turns scaling from a hope into a budget calculation. The prescription that followed was to spend most of any compute increase on parameters and comparatively little on additional tokens, which is exactly the allocation GPT-3 made.

The architecture is GPT-2's, with alternating dense and locally banded sparse attention layers and a context of 2048; the differences are quantitative. The behaviour was not anticipated. Given a task description and a handful of worked examples in the prompt, with no gradient update of any kind, the model performs tasks it was never fine-tuned for, and the gap between zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot widens sharply as the model grows — small models barely benefit from examples, large ones benefit a great deal. The paper argues that skipping fine-tuning is a virtue rather than a shortcut, since a system needing thousands of labelled examples per task is not general. Performance is uneven: strong on closed-book question answering and completion, weak on natural language inference and on comparisons requiring several reasoning steps, and usually still below a fine-tuned model of the same period.

blocks.h: What it cost, and what was wrong
blocks.b: The costs were immediate and structural. Serving 175B dense parameters is expensive per token in a way that training cost, being one-off, is not; the weights were not released; and the corpus was large enough that overlap with evaluation sets had to be measured after the fact rather than excluded in advance. The prescription that fixed the size was itself later overturned. Hoffmann et al. found that parameters and training tokens should grow at roughly the same rate for a fixed compute budget, which makes GPT-3 substantially undertrained — a smaller model on far more data would have been better on quality and on serving cost together. The deeper limitation is one that scale does not touch at all: a model trained to continue text continues the prompt, and does not do what the prompt asks. That is the gap InstructGPT was built to close.

gpt3>instructgpt.lead: GPT-3 would perform a task if the prompt was arranged so that performing it was the most likely continuation. InstructGPT changes what the model optimises, so that following an instruction stops being an artefact of how the context was staged and becomes the objective itself.

blocks.b: In-context learning made capability reachable but not reliable. Next-token prediction over web text is an objective about what people tend to write, not about what a particular user wants; a helpful answer, a fluent fabrication and a continuation that ignores the request entirely are all equally licensed by it. In practice this showed up as a model answering a question with more questions, inventing citations in the same register as true ones, and reproducing the toxicity of its corpus, with "prompt engineering" as the standing workaround — a way of arranging context so that the wanted behaviour happens to be the probable one. The machinery for repairing this already existed outside language modelling: Christiano et al. had optimised policies against a reward model learned from human comparisons, and Stiennon et al. had applied it to summarisation, where it beat supervised fine-tuning on human preference.

Ouyang et al. keep GPT-3 as the initialisation and add a pipeline. Labellers write demonstrations for prompts drawn largely from real API traffic, and supervised fine-tuning yields a first policy. Labellers then rank several sampled completions per prompt, and a reward model $r_\theta$ is fitted to the pairwise comparisons under a Bradley–Terry likelihood, maximising $\log \sigma\!\left(r_\theta(x, y_w) - r_\theta(x, y_l)\right)$ for a preferred completion $y_w$ over a rejected $y_l$. PPO then optimises the policy against $r_\theta$ with a per-token KL penalty back to the supervised model:

$r_\theta(x,y) - \beta \log \frac{\pi(y \mid x)}{\pi^{\mathrm{SFT}}(y \mid x)}$

That penalty is not a matter of taste. Without it the policy drifts into regions where the reward model was never trained, its scores stop tracking anything human, and the samples degrade while the reward rises. Pretraining gradients are mixed back in to limit regression on standard benchmarks.

Labellers preferred the outputs of a 1.3B InstructGPT model to those of 175B GPT-3 — a hundredfold difference in parameters recovered by changing what is optimised rather than how much is trained. That is why every assistant since is a preference-tuned model, and why the technology arrived to the public as a product rather than as an API demonstration. The cost is the substitution at the centre of it. "Human intent" becomes the aggregated judgement of a small contracted labelling pool working to one set of guidelines, and the policy optimises a learned proxy for that judgement, which can be gamed: answers grow longer, more hedged and more agreeable because those properties correlate with approval. Sycophancy and confident wrongness are failure modes of this objective rather than accidents of it. Most of the later work — direct preference optimisation, AI-generated feedback, constitutional methods — is an attempt to keep the alignment while removing the reward model or the labellers.
