Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences
Learning to summarize from human feedback

bert>roberta.lead: RoBERTa adds nothing to BERT's architecture — not a layer, not an activation, not a head. It is a controlled study of BERT's training procedure, and it finds that the original model was undertrained and that one of its two stated objectives was doing no work at all.

blocks.b: BERT arrived as a bundle: a bidirectional encoder, masked-token recovery, next-sentence prediction, a masking pattern generated once during preprocessing, about 16GB of text, and a particular schedule of steps and batch size. Part of the gain was credited to next-sentence prediction, on the reasoning that sentence-pair tasks such as inference and question answering need a discourse-level signal that token-level masking cannot supply. None of these components had been separated from the others, and none of the training choices had been swept. Because pretraining runs were expensive, the field mostly accepted the bundle intact and moved on to architecture — XLNet's permutation objective among them — while comparing new models against BERT's published numbers even when the new models were trained on more data for longer.

Liu et al. hold the architecture fixed and vary one thing at a time. Masking is regenerated on every pass instead of frozen during preprocessing, so a sequence is not seen through the same set of holes on repeated epochs. The input becomes contiguous full sentences packed to the length limit, sampled across document boundaries, and next-sentence prediction is dropped — with everything else matched, removing it slightly improves results rather than degrading them. Batch size rises into the thousands of sequences with a retuned learning rate, the corpus grows roughly tenfold with news, web and story text added, the tokenizer becomes byte-level BPE over a 50k vocabulary, and training simply runs for longer. Each change is reported with the others held constant, which is what makes the conclusions transferable rather than a single lucky configuration.

RoBERTa matched or exceeded XLNet on the standard suites using BERT's exact architecture, which reframed a year of published results: gains attributed to new objectives were partly gains from more data and more optimisation steps, and BERT's own ceiling had never been reached. The practical consequence is that an architectural claim now has to be made at matched compute and matched data, which is expensive enough to be a barrier to entry rather than merely a courtesy. The uncomfortable reading — that a good deal of the apparent progress was budget — recurs at larger scale in the Chinchilla result three years later. What RoBERTa does not touch is anything downstream of the encoder-only choice: the model still cannot generate, still stops at 512 positions, and still trains on `[MASK]` symbols it will never encounter again.

refs.t: RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach
BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers

lstm>seq2seq.lead: LSTM was built to keep a gradient alive across long lags in problems where output is locked to input, one decision per timestep. Seq2Seq kept the cell and broke the lockstep: one LSTM reads a sentence into a vector and never speaks, a second speaks a different sentence out of it.

blocks.b:
Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's contribution was a recurrence whose default behaviour is to leave its memory alone. The cell updates additively,

$c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{c}_t$

so with the forget gate $f_t$ near one the derivative of $c_t$ with respect to $c_{t-1}$ is near one, and error travels back across long spans without the repeated multiplication by a weight matrix that drives it to zero in a plain RNN. The input and output gates decide what is written and what is exposed to the rest of the network; the forget gate, which lets a cell release its memory and gives the update the additive form above, was added three years later by Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins.

What this bought in practice is a sequence model whose state late in a sequence still reflects its beginning. Until 2014 that capacity was spent mostly on aligned tasks — frame-level speech labelling, handwriting recognition, tagging — where the model emits one output per input and never has to hold the whole thing at once.

Sutskever, Vinyals and Le kept the cell and discarded the alignment. Two LSTMs with separate parameters: an encoder that consumes the source and is never asked to emit anything, whose final state is handed to a decoder that runs as a conditional language model, feeding back its own previous output until it produces an end-of-sequence symbol. Input and output lengths become independent, and nothing has to be aligned in advance.

Two additions paid for the removal. Depth — four stacked layers — because one layer's state was too narrow a channel to carry a sentence. And reversing the word order of the source, which places the first source words close in time to the first target words. The paper reports a clear BLEU gain from the reversal alone, which is the sharpest available evidence that the model was limited by how far information had to be carried rather than by capacity. Decoding is a beam search.

Competitive WMT'14 English–French translation from a system with no phrase table, no alignment model and no hand-built features mattered less than the shape the paper established. Any problem mapping one variable-length object to another could now be posed identically, and within two years summarisation, dialogue, image captioning and speech recognition had all been rewritten in encoder-decoder form.

The cost is visible in the architecture. Everything the decoder knows about the source arrives through a single fixed-width vector, so a fifty-word sentence receives the same budget as a five-word one, and quality falls away as sentences lengthen. The reversal trick treated the symptom. Attention, posted within days of it that same autumn, removed the constraint outright by letting the decoder read the encoder's states rather than a summary of them.

refs.t: Long Short-Term Memory
Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks

seq2seq>bahdanau.lead: Seq2Seq made translation one differentiable function, and in doing so localised its own failure to a single object: the vector handed from encoder to decoder. Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio left the encoder-decoder frame intact and replaced that one object with a quantity recomputed at every output step.

blocks.h: A bottleneck you could point at
blocks.b:
The value of the 2014 encoder-decoder was that everything between source text and target text was learned jointly. The price was that the source had to survive as a fixed-width vector, the same size whether the sentence ran to five words or fifty.

Two pieces of evidence made that concrete rather than theoretical. Quality on long sentences fell away relative to phrase-based systems, and reversing the source word order — a change that alters nothing about capacity, only about how far information must travel — produced a real gain. Both point at the same diagnosis: the model was losing the early part of the input rather than failing to represent it. Cho and colleagues measured the degradation against sentence length explicitly, and it was that curve, more than any aggregate score, that defined the target.

The encoder becomes bidirectional and its output is no longer a final state but one annotation $h_j$ per source position, carrying that word together with context from both sides. Before producing word $i$, the decoder scores every annotation against its own previous state using a small feed-forward network, normalises the scores, and takes the weighted sum as its context:

$c_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} h_j$

Nothing here is supervised. The alignment network is trained by the same gradient as the translation, which works only because a soft weighted sum is differentiable where a hard choice of source position would not be.

The recurrence stays. What is thrown away is the requirement that the encoder compress: its states become a memory the decoder can address, so the size of that memory grows with the sentence instead of being fixed in advance.

The length curve flattens — the attention model does not degrade on long sentences the way the fixed-vector model does — and the source-reversal trick becomes unnecessary. The $\alpha$ matrix also turned out to be readable as a soft word alignment, giving the field one of its few legible internal quantities.

The larger consequence is that attention stopped being a translation device. Within two years it was carrying information in image captioning, speech and memory-augmented networks, and pointer and copy mechanisms were built by reading $\alpha$ as a distribution over input positions rather than as a set of weights.

The cost is a score for every source–target pair, so the work grows with the product of the two lengths — quadratic once the two are comparable. More consequentially, attention was still bolted onto a sequential recurrence that dominated wall-clock cost — which is the observation the Transformer acted on.

refs.t: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
On the Properties of Neural Machine Translation: Encoder–Decoder Approaches

nnlm>w2v.lead: Bengio's neural language model learned word vectors as a means to an end: it needed continuous features to smooth a probability estimate over word sequences. Mikolov's group kept the vectors, discarded the probability model, and then removed every part of the network that existed only to serve the discarded part.

blocks.b:
The 2003 model attacks the curse of dimensionality in language modelling. A count-based n-gram has no notion of two words being interchangeable, so an unseen sequence carries no evidence of its own and the model must fall back on smoothing and back-off to shorter contexts to give it any probability at all. Bengio and colleagues gave each word a learned vector, concatenated the vectors of the preceding words, passed them through a tanh hidden layer and a softmax over the whole vocabulary, and trained everything — vectors included — to maximise the likelihood of the next word. Generalisation then comes for free: an unseen combination still receives sensible probability if its words sit near words that were seen there.

The cost was the shape of the network. A dense hidden layer followed by a normalisation over tens of thousands of output words makes every update expensive, and training ran for days on corpora of a few million words. The embeddings were a by-product of an object nobody could afford to scale.

If the embeddings rather than the probabilities are the goal, most of that architecture is overhead. word2vec deletes the hidden layer outright, leaving a model linear between input and output. Skip-gram poses the task backwards — predict each context word from the centre word — so context is a bag rather than an ordered fixed-width window. Negative sampling then removes the softmax: instead of normalising over the vocabulary, train a logistic discriminator between the observed pair and $k$ words drawn from a noise distribution,

$\log\sigma(v'_{w_O}\cdot v_{w_I}) + \sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbb{E}_{w_i\sim P_n}\big[\log\sigma(-v'_{w_i}\cdot v_{w_I})\big]$

with $k$ in the range of five to twenty. The cost of an update no longer depends on vocabulary size at all. Sub-sampling of very frequent words and the fractional-power noise distribution are small empirical additions that mattered more than their size suggests.

The practical change is scale: billions of tokens in hours on one machine, where the neural language model had managed millions in days. Pre-trained vectors became a shared, downloadable resource rather than a per-project expense, and for several years afterwards the first layer of nearly every NLP system was somebody else's embedding table.

Two things were surrendered. The model is no longer a language model — it can place words but not score a sentence — so the estimate that motivated the original work is simply gone. And the same linear structure that produced the well-known analogy behaviour fixes exactly one vector per word type, averaging every sense a word has into a single point weighted by corpus frequency. Contextual embeddings exist because of that second concession.

refs.t: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model
Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality

w2v>glove.lead: GloVe is not a descendant of word2vec but a rival account of why word2vec worked. Pennington, Socher and Manning argued that the useful signal already sat in a corpus-wide co-occurrence matrix, and that sampling local windows one at a time was an indirect way of reaching it.

blocks.b:
word2vec's contribution to this argument was less its algorithm than its result: a shallow objective over raw text yields vectors whose linear structure encodes relations, so analogies can be answered by vector arithmetic. That gave other methods a target to aim at.

It also drew a line the field found suggestive. Count-based methods such as latent semantic analysis factorise a global statistic and were held to do well on similarity but poorly on analogy; prediction-based methods sample local windows and were held to do the reverse. GloVe was written to argue that the line is an artifact of implementation. A window predictor, run over a corpus for several epochs, is only ever accumulating co-occurrence counts one window at a time — so if the counts are the substance, they can be assembled once and factorised directly.

GloVe builds the co-occurrence matrix $X$ in a single pass, then fits vectors so that a dot product reproduces the log count:

$J=\sum_{i,j} f(X_{ij})\big(w_i^\top\tilde w_j + b_i + \tilde b_j - \log X_{ij}\big)^2$

The bias terms absorb per-word frequency, and the weighting $f$ rises with the count and then saturates, so that very frequent pairs cannot dominate the objective; zero entries are skipped entirely.

The derivation begins from ratios of co-occurrence probabilities — what distinguishes ice from steam is not the probability of solid near each but the ratio between them — and a model whose dot products are differences of logs makes such ratios linear in the space by construction. What is kept from word2vec is the target property, linear analogy structure. What is discarded is the sampling: training runs over non-zero matrix entries, not over corpus positions.

GloVe reported higher analogy accuracy than skip-gram at matched dimensionality, and its released vectors — including a 300-dimensional set trained on Common Crawl — became a default first layer for several years, used interchangeably with word2vec's.

The theoretical claim did not survive intact. Levy and Goldberg showed that skip-gram with negative sampling is implicitly factorising a shifted pointwise-mutual-information matrix, which makes it a count method in different clothes. A follow-up study attributed most of the reported gaps between embedding methods to hyperparameters — window size, number of negatives, context symmetry, whether both vectors are summed — rather than to the objectives themselves.

The honest summary is that the two routes arrive at much the same place, and both stop at the same wall: one vector per word type, and a matrix that must be rebuilt to add data.

refs.t: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation
Neural Word Embedding as Implicit Matrix Factorization
Improving Distributional Similarity with Lessons Learned from Word Embeddings

w2v>fasttext.lead: fastText comes out of Facebook AI Research, with word2vec's lead author among its four, and leaves the skip-gram objective untouched. What it replaces is the thing being embedded: a word stops being an atom with its own row in a table and becomes a sum of its character n-grams, so a word the corpus never contained still has a vector.

blocks.h: A lookup table and its edge
blocks.b:
Skip-gram's arrangement is a table indexed by word type. Each type owns an input vector, fitted by the negative-sampling objective from the contexts in which that exact string appeared. The arrangement is what makes training cheap and what fixes the limits.

A type seen twice gets a vector fitted from two observations; a type not seen at all has no row, and the usual workaround was to collapse everything below a frequency threshold into a single unknown symbol. The table also has no way of knowing that walk, walking, walked and walker are related — each is a separate index, and the relationship must be rediscovered from context statistics independently for every form. In English that is a mild inefficiency. In Turkish, Finnish or Czech, where a lemma may surface in dozens of forms, most forms are rare and the model is short of evidence for nearly all of them.

Bojanowski and colleagues keep the context vectors, the negative sampling and the training loop, and change only how a word's input vector is formed. The word is padded with boundary symbols and decomposed into character n-grams of length three to six, plus the full word itself. Each n-gram carries a vector, and the score against a context word becomes

$s(w,c)=\sum_{g\in G_w} z_g^\top v_c$

Because distinct n-grams run into the millions, they are hashed into a fixed bucket table, which bounds memory at the price of collisions.

The removal that had to be paid for is the guarantee of a private row per word: a representation is now shared with every other word sharing its substrings. For inflected and compounding languages that sharing is exactly the right inductive bias, and the reported gains on word-similarity benchmarks concentrate there rather than in English.

The out-of-vocabulary problem largely disappears. A vector for an unseen word, a typo or a novel compound can be composed at test time from parts the model has seen. Together with byte-pair encoding, which arrived in machine translation at almost the same moment, this settled a question the field has not reopened: the unit of text is a sub-word, not a word.

It is worth being precise about what did not change. The limitation word2vec left behind was one vector per type and therefore no polysemy, and fastText inherits it whole — composing from characters still produces a single context-independent vector. Character overlap is also not meaning: unrelated strings that share n-grams are pulled together, non-compositional words are the worst case, and the hash table adds collisions of its own.

refs.t: Enriching Word Vectors with Subword Information
Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units

lstm>elmo.lead: ELMo is an LSTM language model put to a different use. Peters and colleagues trained stacked bidirectional LSTMs on a large corpus with nothing but the next-word objective, then froze them and used their internal states — all of them, not only the top — as the input representation for other tasks.

blocks.b:
By 2017 the gated recurrent cell had settled into a role. A large stacked LSTM was the strongest language model anyone could train, and the scaling work of that period had shown that a billion words and very wide layers kept improving perplexity rather than saturating.

Two properties made ELMo possible. The cell carries state across a whole sentence, so the representation of a token is a function of everything that preceded it — context-dependence, which is the entire point. And the architecture stacks: a deep recurrent model develops layers that compute recognisably different things rather than one undifferentiated mixture. The second property is what makes the mixing weights worth having at all. If every layer computed the same quantity there would be nothing to weight, and ELMo would collapse into ordinary feature extraction from a top layer.

The unusual choice is that ELMo does not take the top layer. For each token it retains every layer's state, from the character-CNN input upwards, and lets the downstream task learn a normalised mixture over them:

$\mathrm{ELMo}_k^{\mathrm{task}} = \gamma^{\mathrm{task}}\sum_{j=0}^{L} s_j^{\mathrm{task}}\, h_{k,j}$

where the $s_j$ are softmax-normalised weights and $\gamma$ a scale. Probing showed why this pays: lower layers carry more syntax, higher layers more word sense, and different tasks want different blends.

Bidirectionality is handled by training a forward and a backward language model separately and concatenating their states layer by layer. That is a compromise the objective forces — one network cannot both condition on the right-hand context and be asked to predict it. The mixture is then fed to an existing task model whose architecture is otherwise left alone.

Adding ELMo improved every one of the six benchmarks the paper tried — question answering, entailment, semantic role labelling, coreference, named entities, sentiment — usually by margins that task-specific architecture tuning had stopped producing. The lesson drawn was general: a large unsupervised model is a better source of features than any hand-designed encoder, and the labelled dataset should be spent on the task rather than on learning the language.

Its own limits set the following year's agenda. The two directions are trained apart and joined only by concatenation, so no layer ever conditions on both sides at once. The model is used frozen, as features, rather than fine-tuned. And the LSTM is sequential, which caps the volume of text that can be pushed through it. BERT is a direct answer to all three.

refs.t: Deep Contextualized Word Representations
Exploring the Limits of Language Modeling

w2v>elmo.lead: word2vec established the interface that NLP used for half a decade: a table mapping word type to dense vector, trained once on unlabelled text and dropped in as somebody else's first layer. ELMo kept the interface and replaced the table with a function of the sentence the word is standing in.

blocks.b:
Two things travelled from word2vec, and only one of them is the vectors. The first is the demonstration that an objective over raw text — no labels, no annotation — yields representations that improve supervised systems trained on quite different tasks. The second is the shape of that transfer: a lookup table, initialised from a downloaded file, sitting under whatever architecture the task called for.

That interface was extremely convenient, and its convenience is what fixed the problem. A lookup is a function of the word type alone, so `bank`, `play` and `bear` each get one point that must average all their senses, weighted by how often each occurs. Attempts to repair this inside the table — clustering a word's contexts and issuing a fixed number of sense vectors per word — required deciding in advance how many senses a word has, and never took hold.

ELMo keeps the interface and changes what sits behind it. A token's representation is produced by running a pre-trained bidirectional language model over the entire sentence and mixing its layer states, so the same string receives different vectors in different sentences and disambiguation is continuous rather than a choice from a fixed inventory.

In practice ELMo did not even displace the static vectors. The standard recipe concatenates them, $[x_k;\ \mathrm{ELMo}_k]$, keeping the type-level information and adding the contextual signal on top. What had to be supplied to make the substitution work was a training signal rich enough to learn context at all: word2vec's shallow window objective cannot, while a language-model objective on a deep recurrent network can. CoVe had shown the same effect a year earlier using a translation encoder, at the cost of requiring a parallel corpus.

The static-embedding era closed quickly. Within about a year the leaderboards for question answering, entailment and tagging belonged to contextual models, and pre-trained word vectors survived mainly as baselines or as one input among several.

What was surrendered is exactly the property that made word2vec infrastructure. A lookup is free at inference and can be precomputed; a contextual representation demands a forward pass over a deep sequence model for every sentence, every time, and there is no per-type vector left to cache or to inspect. Compactness went with it — an embedding file needed no runtime, whereas ELMo ships a model. Later analysis also found contextual vector spaces strongly anisotropic, concentrated in a narrow cone, which makes the geometric intuitions built on static embeddings an unreliable guide.

refs.t: Deep Contextualized Word Representations
Learned in Translation: Contextualized Word Vectors
How Contextual are Contextualized Word Representations?

bahdanau>attnmech.lead: Bahdanau et al. built one mechanism for one job: letting a translation decoder re-read the source instead of working from a single summary vector. What the field extracted from it is smaller and far more general — a differentiable lookup with no commitment to translation, to recurrence, or even to sequences.

blocks.b: The decoder computes a weighted read over all encoder states, $c_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} h_j$, with $\alpha_i$ a softmax over scores $e_{ij} = a(s_{i-1}, h_j)$ produced by a small feed-forward network. What lifts this above an engineering fix is that the selection is soft and therefore **differentiable**. Choosing which source word to read is a discrete decision carrying no gradient; the softmax replaces it with a convex combination, so error at the output reaches every candidate in proportion to how much it was used, and the alignment is learned from the translation loss alone, with no alignment supervision anywhere in the pipeline. Content-based addressing had been proposed at almost the same moment in the Neural Turing Machine; Bahdanau's version was the one that arrived attached to a translation result the field could not ignore.

The generalisation discards nearly everything specific. The query need not be a decoder state, the attended set need not be a sentence or ordered at all, and the scorer need not be a feed-forward network — Luong et al. showed a plain dot product served as well. The one structural addition is a split Bahdanau did not need: he used $h_j$ both as the thing matched against and the thing summed, where the primitive separates a **key**, used for scoring, from a **value**, used for content.

$\mathrm{Attn}(q, K, V) = \sum_j \frac{\exp s(q, k_j)}{\sum_l \exp s(q, k_l)}\, v_j$

Here $q$ is whatever is asking, $k_j$ what each slot advertises, $v_j$ what it returns, and $s$ any differentiable score. Written this way it is a dictionary addressed by content rather than by position, returning a blend rather than an entry.

blocks.h: Where it went, and what it cost
blocks.b:
Read as addressing rather than alignment, it spread within about two years: captioning models attending over convolutional feature maps, pointer networks whose output is the $\alpha$ vector itself, memory networks, and then self-attention, where queries and keys are drawn from the same set and the recurrence attention was invented to assist disappears entirely.

Two costs came with it. Scoring every query against every key is quadratic in set size — invisible for a thirty-token sentence, and now the binding constraint on context length. And the legibility of the alignments, the property that made the mechanism persuasive in 2015, proved a weaker claim than it looked: attention weights are not a faithful account of what a model used, and one can often find quite different weights leaving the prediction unchanged. The dispute over that ran through 2019 without a clean verdict.

transformer>detr.lead: DETR is a genuine join of two lineages that had no prior contact: a Transformer encoder–decoder built for translation, and object detection's long attempt to be rid of anchors and non-maximum suppression. What the Transformer supplied was not attention as such but a decoder emitting several outputs at once, each able to see the others before committing.

blocks.b: A Transformer decoder layer runs two attention paths: cross-attention into the encoder memory, and self-attention among its own positions. In translation the second enforces fluency between output tokens. In detection it does something convolutional pipelines had only reached for at the margins — it lets a fixed set of candidate predictions communicate before any of them is scored, the job non-maximum suppression was doing by hand after the fact, and the job learned-NMS and Relation Networks had already attacked with attention between proposals. The cross-attention is global at the first layer, so the receptive-field problem that convolutional detectors patched with feature pyramids, dilations and context modules does not arise. And because the decoder need not be run autoregressively, all outputs can be produced in one pass. That last freedom is what forces the rest of the design: parallel outputs have no canonical order, so the usual per-anchor supervision has nothing to attach to.

blocks.h: What DETR kept and what it added
blocks.b: A ResNet backbone stays — the fusion is literal, with convolutional features flattened into a sequence and given positional encodings before the Transformer sees them. Anchors, NMS and autoregressive decoding all go. Two things are added to make the removal survive. The decoder's input is a set of **learned object queries**, roughly a hundred free embeddings that carry no image content and act as slots each prediction is written into. And the loss becomes a **bipartite matching**: the Hungarian algorithm finds the least-cost one-to-one assignment between predictions and ground-truth boxes, using a cost combining class probability, an $\ell_1$ box term and generalised IoU, and gradients flow only through that assignment. Unmatched slots are trained to predict no object. Set prediction with Hungarian matching had been tried before, for people detection in crowds; it had never had an architecture whose outputs could coordinate well enough to exploit it.

blocks.h: What it changed, and the bill
blocks.b:
It reframed detection as set prediction with learned queries, and that framing took over: Deformable DETR, DINO, and the query-based segmentation and tracking heads that followed all inherit it. The pipeline became genuinely end-to-end, with no post-processing stage whose thresholds needed tuning per dataset.

The costs were immediate and severe. DETR needed on the order of five hundred epochs on COCO where a Faster R-CNN baseline trains in a few dozen, because cross-attention starts near-uniform over the feature map and must learn sparsity from scratch. Small-object accuracy was clearly worse, the original having no multi-scale features. The fixed query count caps recall in crowded scenes. Deformable DETR fixed convergence and small objects with sparse learned sampling offsets and a multi-scale encoder — which is to say some of the hand-built geometric prior came back in.

transformer>vit.lead: ViT moves the Transformer into vision with as little modification as its authors could manage, and the smallness of the change is the argument. Cutting an image into 16×16 patches and treating each as a token is the entire transplant; everything of interest lies in what that discards and what has to pay for it.

blocks.b: The Transformer is a sequence model with no locality assumption: every position reaches every other in one step, at the first layer, and its cost is dense matrix multiplication rather than a sequential loop. For vision the appeal was obvious and the obstacle was arithmetic. Attention is $O(n^2)$ in the number of tokens, and a $224 \times 224$ image has 50,176 pixels, so pixels-as-tokens is not merely expensive but impossible at that resolution. Every earlier attempt worked around this: non-local blocks and attention-augmented convolutions kept the convolutional stack and added attention on top; other work restricted attention to local windows or to very small images. What the transplant needed was not a new mechanism but a tokenisation coarse enough to bring $n$ into the range the Transformer already handled for sentences.

Split the image into non-overlapping patches of side $P$, giving

$N = HW/P^2$

tokens — 196 for a 224-pixel image at $P = 16$, comfortably a sentence length. Each patch is flattened and linearly projected, learned position embeddings are added, a class token is prepended, and from there it is an unmodified encoder. Thrown away with the convolution: translation equivariance, locality, and the hierarchical scale pyramid — essentially the entire visual prior accumulated since LeNet. What pays for the removal is data. Trained on ImageNet-1k alone, ViT trails a comparable ResNet; at ImageNet-21k it draws level; pretrained on JFT-300M it passes it. The paper's claim is that inductive bias is a substitute for data and, above some scale, an inferior one. The attention maps support it: early layers learn local heads, relearning locality where locality pays.

The lasting consequence is architectural consolidation. One backbone now serves text, images, audio and video, which is what makes joint training across modalities practical — CLIP-style dual encoders and the vision towers of multimodal language models all sit on this.

The specific claim about data did not survive intact. DeiT reached competitive accuracy on ImageNet-1k alone using distillation and heavy augmentation, showing the three hundred million images were partly a stand-in for a training recipe. ConvNeXt then modernised a ResNet with the same recipe and matched ViT at comparable scale, which suggests a good deal of the original gap was schedule and augmentation rather than architecture. What remains is the cost: quadratic growth with resolution and no native multi-scale structure, which Swin addressed by reintroducing windows and a hierarchy.

bert>beit.lead: BEiT transplants the masked-language objective almost literally: hide part of the input, predict the identity of what was hidden, cross-entropy over a vocabulary. The awkwardness is that images have no vocabulary, and BEiT's answer was to borrow one from elsewhere.

blocks.b: BERT gave up left-to-right factorisation in order to condition on both sides of a token, and paid for it with a corrupted-input pretext task: mask a small fraction of tokens and recover them from context. The transferable shape of that idea is domain-neutral — corrupt, predict what was removed, then discard the prediction head and keep the encoder. But the version that worked carried a quiet dependency. The target is a categorical draw from a fixed discrete vocabulary of around thirty thousand WordPiece units, which makes the loss a well-scaled classification with an unambiguous answer, and makes the task hard in a useful way: a missing word generally cannot be reconstructed by smoothing its neighbours. Neither property holds for a patch of pixels, and every masked-image method is in effect an argument about how to restore them.

BEiT keeps the loss and supplies the missing discreteness from outside. The discrete VAE trained for DALL-E is frozen and used as a tokeniser: each 16×16 patch maps to one index in an 8192-entry codebook. An image therefore has two views — patch embeddings, which are the encoder's input, and visual tokens, which are the target. Masking is blockwise rather than scattered, covering up to roughly forty percent of patches, because an isolated masked patch is recoverable by low-level continuation from its neighbours and teaches nothing. The encoder is a plain ViT; the head is a softmax over codebook indices and is thrown away afterwards. What is kept from BERT is the whole corrupt-and-classify structure. What is added is an entire external pretraining stage, trained separately and on other data, sitting upstream of the objective.

BEiT established masked image modelling as a serious alternative to the contrastive and siamese methods that then dominated visual self-supervision, which needed carefully tuned augmentations, negatives or momentum teachers. Masking needs none of that machinery.

It also made clear what the real design variable was: not the mask, but the reconstruction target. The descendants split on exactly that. MAE removed the tokeniser altogether and predicted raw pixels, showing the discreteness BERT depended on was not required so long as the mask was aggressive enough. BEiT v2 went the other way, replacing the DALL-E codebook with a semantically richer teacher to get better linear-probe features. The cost of the original is that the pipeline is not self-contained — its results are partly the tokeniser's results, and the codebook fixes in advance the semantic level at which the model is asked to predict.

bert>mae.lead: MAE takes BERT's objective and asks a sharper question about it: why the mask ratio that suits language does not suit images. Its answer — that images are spatially redundant in a way that text is not — licenses hiding three-quarters of the patches, and an asymmetric encoder is what makes that affordable rather than merely correct.

blocks.h: What the recipe assumed about text
blocks.b: BERT masks roughly fifteen percent of tokens, and the figure is tuned to a signal where each token carries a great deal of information and is hard to guess: remove a word and the gap generally cannot be closed by continuing its neighbours. Two further properties of language are baked in and invisible until the objective is moved. The encoder processes the full sequence, mask placeholders included, which is cheap when the mask is small. And the prediction head can be a single linear layer, because the target is a word — an object already at the semantic level the representation is meant to reach. Carried into vision unaltered, the first assumption makes pretraining expensive and the second makes the task easy in the wrong way, since a lightly masked patch can be interpolated from its surroundings without any understanding at all.

blocks.h: Two changes, each enabling the other
blocks.b: The mask ratio goes to seventy-five percent, which removes enough of the image that low-level extrapolation cannot solve it and the model must infer content from distant context. That would be prohibitively slow with BERT's arrangement, so the encoder is changed to see only the visible quarter of patches — mask tokens are not fed to it at all. A shallow decoder then receives the full set, encoded visible tokens plus a shared learned mask token with positional embeddings, reconstructs pixels for the masked positions only, and is discarded after pretraining. Because attention is quadratic and the encoder carries nearly all the parameters, dropping three-quarters of its tokens cuts wall-clock training time several-fold. The decoder must be non-trivial, unlike BERT's linear head, precisely because pixels sit far below the level of the representation being learned.

What results is the plainest recipe in visual self-supervision: no tokeniser, no negatives, no momentum teacher, no elaborate augmentation policy. It scales cleanly with model size, and a ViT-Huge pretrained this way fine-tunes to just under eighty-eight percent top-1 on ImageNet-1k without any external data. The same construction carried directly to video, audio spectrograms and point clouds, and masked pretraining became the default for large vision backbones.

The catch is in what the representation is good for. MAE's features are markedly weaker under linear probing than those from contrastive methods, because reconstructing pixels leaves low-level detail in the encoder that a linear classifier cannot exploit; the model has to be fine-tuned to show its quality. The pretext task therefore dictates the evaluation protocol, which is a limitation MAE passed on rather than solved.

elman>lstm.lead: Elman's recurrent network made time a structural property of the model rather than a fixed window over the input. It also made the gradient a long product of Jacobians, and the LSTM is a precisely targeted answer to that product and to almost nothing else in Elman's design.

blocks.b:
Elman fed the hidden layer back as context units, so in principle the state at step $t$ depends on every input before it. Trained by backpropagation through time, error at step $T$ reaches step $t$ through

$\prod_{k=t+1}^{T} \frac{\partial h_k}{\partial h_{k-1}}$

where each factor is the recurrent weight matrix multiplied by the derivative of a saturating nonlinearity, itself bounded well below one. The product therefore shrinks geometrically over span, and weights large enough to prevent that make it explode instead. Hochreiter's 1991 thesis and Bengio and colleagues in 1994 established that this is structural rather than an optimisation nuisance: with squashing units one cannot have both stable forward dynamics and gradients surviving tens of steps. In practice Elman networks learned dependencies a handful of steps long, which is a window with extra machinery.

blocks.h: A path where the Jacobian is one
blocks.b: Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's answer was to build one route through the network along which the Jacobian is exactly the identity: a linear self-connected memory cell with recurrent weight fixed at 1, so that $c_t = c_{t-1} + \ldots$ and $\partial c_t / \partial c_{t-1} = 1$. Error travelling that route neither decays nor explodes — their constant error carousel. A cell that accumulates everything is useless, so multiplicative gates guard it: an input gate deciding what may be written, an output gate deciding what may be read, each a sigmoid of the current input and previous state. Recurrence and BPTT are kept; what is abandoned is Elman's assumption that memory and nonlinearity live in the same unit. Worth being exact: the 1997 model had no forget gate and could not release what it had stored. Gers and colleagues added it two years later, making the decay learned as $\prod_k f_k$ rather than fixed by the weights.

blocks.h: What it enabled and what it did not touch
blocks.b:
Dependencies over hundreds of steps became learnable: LSTMs were already winning handwriting recognition competitions by 2009, and after 2013 they carried speech recognition, sequence-to-sequence translation and neural language modelling — effectively the whole stack that preceded the Transformer.

The price was roughly four times the parameters per unit at equal state width, and gate arithmetic at every timestep. More importantly, the fix addressed the gradient and left the other property of recurrence untouched: step $t$ still cannot begin before step $t-1$ has finished, so training time scales with sequence length no matter how much hardware is available. That is the limitation the Transformer was built to remove, and it is why LSTMs lost their position despite working. The additive path itself outlived the architecture — it is the same argument residual connections later made about depth rather than time.

lstm>gru.lead: The GRU is a subtraction. Cho and colleagues kept the gated additive update that lets gradients survive and cut away as much of the surrounding apparatus as they could — the separate cell state, the output gate, the independent write and erase decisions — to find out which parts were carrying their weight.

blocks.h: What had been shown, and what had not
blocks.b: By 2014 the LSTM cell had accumulated input, forget and output gates and, in common variants, peephole connections, with no systematic account of which components mattered. One part was clearly load-bearing: the state is updated by accumulation rather than recomputed through a squashing nonlinearity, so the Jacobian along the memory path stays near the identity and can be modulated by a learned gate. Everything else was plausible and unaudited. Cho and colleagues came at the question from a practical direction rather than an analytical one — they needed a recurrent encoder–decoder to score phrase pairs for a statistical machine translation system, and a unit with fewer parameters and a shorter critical path was worth having on its own terms. The reduction was proposed as an engineering economy and became an experiment about necessity.

The cell and hidden state are merged into a single vector, so there is nothing left to gate on the way out and the output gate disappears. Writing and forgetting are coupled into one update gate, making the state an interpolation:

$h_t = (1 - z_t) \odot h_{t-1} + z_t \odot \tilde{h}_t$

where $z_t$ is the update gate, $h_{t-1}$ the previous state and $\tilde{h}_t$ the candidate. A reset gate $r_t$ controls how much of $h_{t-1}$ the candidate is allowed to see when it is computed. Three weight matrices remain where the LSTM has four, about a quarter fewer parameters per unit. The coupling is the substantive change, not merely a saving: because the same $z_t$ appears as both $1 - z_t$ and $z_t$, retaining the old state and writing a new one are one decision, and the state stays a convex combination of bounded quantities. The LSTM cell has no such bound.

It did not, in any decisive way. The authors' own evaluation, and the larger sweeps by Greff and by Jozefowicz and colleagues shortly after, found no consistent winner across tasks; what they did find was that the forget gate and the initialisation of its bias matter more than most of the variations people had proposed, and that many variants are interchangeable.

Where a clean separation exists it favours the LSTM, and it follows from the boundedness above: a state confined to a convex combination cannot grow without limit, so a GRU cannot implement an unbounded counter while an LSTM's additive cell can. That shows up on formal-language tasks and rarely on natural data. The practical verdict was that GRUs are the better default when data or compute are short. The interpolation form outlived the argument entirely — highway networks took it into feedforward depth, and gated accumulation returns in the selective state-space models.

transformer>moe.lead: A Transformer block is attention followed by a position-wise feed-forward network, and it is the feed-forward network that holds most of the parameters and multiplies every token by the same dense matrix. Sparse MoE replaces that one network with many copies and a router that wakes only a couple of them per token, breaking the assumption that more parameters must mean more arithmetic. The chronology is awkward and worth stating plainly: Shazeer's gated MoE layer was published months before the Transformer and sat between stacked LSTM layers. It was the Transformer's feed-forward slot that gave the idea somewhere to live.

blocks.b:
Inside a Transformer layer the feed-forward network is

$\mathrm{FFN}(x) = W_2\,\sigma(W_1 x)$

applied independently at every position, with the hidden width $d_{\mathrm{ff}}$ conventionally four times $d_{\mathrm{model}}$. Counting parameters per layer, attention contributes four $d^2$ blocks and the feed-forward network eight, so roughly two thirds of the weights sit in a component that never looks at another position.

Two properties follow, and both are what conditional computation needs. First, the block is genuinely **position-wise**: nothing inside it couples tokens, so choosing a different set of weights for each token breaks no dependency. Second, its cost per token is exactly proportional to its parameter count. Under the scaling behaviour that motivated the whole enterprise, quality tracked parameters, and every additional parameter was additional arithmetic on every token processed, in training and forever afterwards in serving. That proportionality was the constraint, not the capacity.

Sparse MoE keeps the block-shaped structure and replaces the single feed-forward network with $n$ experts and a gate:

$y = \sum_{i=1}^{n} G(x)_i\, E_i(x), \qquad G(x) = \mathrm{softmax}(\mathrm{TopK}(x W_g + \epsilon,\, k))$

where $E_i$ are the experts, $W_g$ is a small learned routing matrix, $\epsilon$ is tunable noise, and $\mathrm{TopK}$ sets all but the $k$ largest logits to $-\infty$. A gate value of zero means the expert is never evaluated, so cost per token scales with $k$ rather than $n$.

Removing the dense multiply required two additions. The noise in the gate exists so that routing can be explored rather than frozen at initialisation. More importantly an auxiliary balancing loss is needed, because routing is self-reinforcing: whichever expert is picked early gets more gradient, gets better, and gets picked more. Left alone, the layer collapses onto a handful of experts and the rest are dead weight.

Parameter count and per-token arithmetic came apart, and the currency of scale shifted from FLOPs to memory and interconnect bandwidth. Everything sparse at the frontier descends from this layer occupying the feed-forward slot — GShard, Switch, GLaM, and the mixture-of-experts models that now dominate large open releases.

The costs are real. Every expert must be resident even though few run, so a sparse model is cheap in compute and expensive in memory. Experts are sharded across devices, which puts an all-to-all exchange in the middle of every layer and makes throughput sensitive to batch composition. Experts are provisioned with a fixed capacity, so tokens are dropped when routing is uneven. Training destabilises because the router's exponentials are numerically fragile in low precision.

And one quieter consequence: **parameter count stopped being comparable across models**. An announced trillion parameters may cost less per token than a dense ten billion.

refs.t: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
Attention Is All You Need

moe>switch.lead: Shazeer's MoE layer routed each token to at least two experts, and the paper argued this was necessary: with a single expert the gate receives no comparative signal and cannot learn to choose. Switch Transformer showed the argument did not hold, and that the simplification it unlocked was what let sparsity survive contact with a large Transformer training stack.

blocks.b:
The sparsely-gated layer arrived with its machinery already identified: noisy top-$k$ gating, an auxiliary loss to keep experts equally used, and expert parallelism across devices. It worked, at billions of parameters, inside stacked LSTM translation models.

What it left were engineering problems that grew with scale rather than shrinking. Routing to $k$ experts means $k$ copies of each token's activation crossing the network, $k$ dispatches, and a weighted combine on the way back — the all-to-all exchange, not the arithmetic, becomes the bottleneck. Expert capacity has to be provisioned in advance and is wasted or overflowed depending on how balanced routing happens to be. The balancing losses were fragile, and training in reduced precision was unreliable.

There was also a gap in evidence. GShard had already run the layer inside a 600-billion-parameter Transformer for multilingual translation, so what was missing was not a Transformer demonstration but a version simple and stable enough to drop into a general-purpose pre-training stack.

Switch sets $k = 1$. Each token goes to exactly one expert. Communication volume and activation memory halve, expert capacity halves, and the combine collapses to multiplying the expert's output by its router probability — which is also the answer to the original objection. The gradient reaches the router through that scalar, and because the softmax normalises over all experts, the unchosen ones still shape it.

Three additions make the removal survive. An explicit capacity factor, with tokens beyond an expert's budget dropped and passed through the residual connection rather than stalling the batch. A differentiable balancing loss

$\ell = \alpha N \sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i P_i$

where $N$ is the number of experts, $f_i$ the fraction of tokens dispatched to expert $i$, and $P_i$ the mean router probability assigned to it; the product is minimised at uniform routing. And selective precision — the router computed in float32 while everything else runs in bfloat16 — because the router's exponentials are exactly where low precision diverges. Reduced initialisation scale did the rest.

Switch reported large pre-training speedups over a dense T5 baseline at matched compute, and scaled a language model past a trillion parameters with thousands of experts. More durably, it fixed the vocabulary: capacity factor, expert dropping, auxiliary balance loss and float32 routing are now the standard dials, and top-1 became the default assumption a design has to argue its way out of.

The costs were equally clarifying. Quality became dependent on batch composition, since whether a token is dropped depends on the other tokens it travels with. Fine-tuning overfitted badly, needing expert-specific dropout to control. Memory footprint made the models unservable outside large clusters, and distilling a sparse teacher back into a dense student recovered only part of the gain.

Later work stepped back off the extreme. Mixtral returned to top-2, and subsequent designs use finer-grained experts with shared always-on ones — but they argue against a baseline Switch defined.

refs.t: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
GShard: Scaling Giant Models with Conditional Computation and Automatic Sharding

switch>mixtral.lead: Switch settled the question of whether a sparse Transformer can be trained at extreme scale. What it produced was a research artefact in an encoder-decoder research stack, needing a pod of accelerators to hold. Mixtral took the same layer and shrank the ambition until the result was something an ordinary organisation could download, serve and fine-tune.

blocks.b:
By the time Switch was done, the recipe was no longer speculative. Substitute a mixture layer for the feed-forward network, route each token with a small learned gate, provision each expert with a fixed capacity, hold the balance with an auxiliary loss, and compute the router in float32. Sparse pre-training beat dense pre-training at matched arithmetic, repeatedly and at several scales.

The negative results were just as informative. Thousands of experts must be spread across many hosts, which puts a cross-host all-to-all inside every layer and makes the model inseparable from the cluster it was trained on. Token dropping ties quality to batching. Fine-tuning is unstable. Nothing about a 1.6-trillion-parameter checkpoint is servable by anyone without the same hardware.

So the open question after Switch was not whether sparsity works. It was **what shape of sparsity is servable**.

Mixtral keeps the layer and changes nearly every quantity attached to it. Eight experts per layer instead of thousands, present in every layer, with top-2 routing rather than top-1. Around 47 billion parameters in total, of which roughly 13 billion are active for any given token. The surrounding decoder is deliberately conventional and Llama-shaped — RMSNorm, SwiGLU, rotary position embeddings, grouped-query attention — with a 32k context, and the weights were released under Apache 2.0 with no usage clause attached.

The eight-expert choice is the design. All experts fit within a single node's memory, so the all-to-all exchange never leaves the host and the model can be served with ordinary tensor parallelism. Returning to top-2 restores an actual mixture per token and softens the routing brittleness that top-1 introduces.

The paper's routing analysis is worth repeating because it is a negative result honestly reported: experts show little topical specialisation. There is no maths expert and no code expert. What the routing does show is positional structure — consecutive tokens are often sent to the same expert.

Mixtral 8x7B was reported as matching or beating Llama 2 70B across most of the benchmarks its authors evaluated, using roughly a fifth of the active parameters. That reframed sparsity as a serving argument rather than a training-efficiency argument, and forced the open tooling ecosystem — inference servers, quantisation formats, fine-tuning libraries — to support mixtures rather than treat them as an exotic case.

The cost is that memory, not arithmetic, becomes the binding constraint. Forty-seven billion parameters must be resident to use thirteen, so the model is cheap for a datacentre serving many concurrent requests and offers nothing to a single user with one consumer GPU. The throughput advantage only materialises at batch sizes large enough that every expert has work to do; below that, a sparse model is a dense model that wasted its memory. Quantisation and low-rank fine-tuning both had to be reconsidered per-expert, and adapters that assume one feed-forward network per layer simply do not apply.

refs.t: Mixtral of Experts
Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity

llama>alpaca.lead: LLaMA shipped a capable base model with no instruction-following behaviour whatsoever: it continued text and nothing else. Alpaca and Vicuna demonstrated that the missing layer was remarkably thin — a few tens of thousands of demonstrations, borrowed from a model that had already been aligned, bought most of the visible chat behaviour for a few hundred dollars.

blocks.b:
Two things had to be true at once for what followed, and LLaMA was the first release where both were. The model was strong at 7 and 13 billion parameters, small enough to fine-tune fully on hardware a university lab already owned. And the weights were on disk — nominally released to approved researchers, in practice everywhere within a week.

The deeper precondition is about what instruction tuning actually is. FLAN and InstructGPT had already shown that a modest amount of instruction and preference data reshapes how a base model responds; the stronger claim that fine-tuning merely elicits a format latent in pre-training came later, with LIMA, and is still argued over. The base model can already answer the question; it simply has no reason to believe that answering is what comes next rather than another plausible paragraph of web text. If eliciting a latent format is all that is required, the fine-tuning set can be small. What was missing until LLaMA was an open base model good enough to have anything worth eliciting.

Alpaca applied the Self-Instruct pipeline: start from 175 seed tasks written by hand, expand them with a commercial instruction-tuned model into 52,000 instruction–response pairs, then supervised fine-tune LLaMA-7B on the result. The total came to under six hundred dollars, most of it API calls rather than compute, with the training itself a few hours on eight accelerators.

Vicuna took a different source — roughly 70,000 multi-turn conversations that users had shared publicly from their own sessions with a commercial chatbot — and fine-tuned the 13B model, reporting around ninety per cent of the reference chatbot's quality as judged by a stronger model.

What was discarded is the striking part: reward modelling, preference collection, and reinforcement learning from human feedback, the entire apparatus InstructGPT had established as necessary. In its place is imitation of a model that had already been through that apparatus. Almost nothing had to be added to make the removal work, and that is precisely the finding.

Instruction tuning became a weekend project, and hundreds of derivative models followed within months. Low-rank adaptation plus synthetic instruction data settled in as the default recipe for turning any base model into an assistant.

The evaluation was the weak joint, and the field said so within the year. Work on imitating proprietary models found that imitation transfers **style rather than substance** — the confident register, the structured answer, the appropriate length — while factual and reasoning gaps against the teacher persist and sometimes widen with more imitation data. Both crowdworkers and model judges reward exactly the surface properties that transfer easily, so the headline quality figures measured the thing that was cheapest to acquire.

Two further costs stuck. Distilling outputs from a commercial API sits uneasily against its terms of service, which shaped how later open models described their data. And shared-conversation corpora circulate into benchmarks, making contamination difficult to rule out. What remains is a sharper distinction between eliciting a capability and creating one.

refs.t: Self-Instruct: Aligning Language Models with Self-Generated Instructions
Alpaca: A Strong, Replicable Instruction-Following Model
The False Promise of Imitating Proprietary LLMs
Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena

llama>llama2.lead: LLaMA-1 was a base model under a research-only licence with alignment explicitly deferred to whoever downloaded it. LLaMA-2 changed the architecture very little and instead supplied the two things that made the lineage usable in production: a licence permitting commercial deployment, and a complete preference-tuning pipeline shipped in the box. It also quietly withdrew the data transparency that had been LLaMA-1's stated justification.

blocks.b:
The first release settled a technical question and created a social fact. Technically, it showed that training small models far past the compute-optimal point on entirely public corpora yields models competitive with far larger closed ones, and it fixed a concrete architectural shape — pre-normalisation with RMSNorm, SwiGLU activations, rotary position embeddings — that the open community adopted more or less wholesale as the default decoder.

Socially, the derivative explosion demonstrated demand that no lab had measured before. Within weeks there were instruction-tuned variants, quantised runtimes for consumer hardware and adapter libraries built specifically around the checkpoint shapes.

It also demonstrated the limits of shipping a base model alone. There was no chat behaviour, no multi-turn instruction adherence, no refusal behaviour of any kind, and a licence that barred anyone from building a product on it. Every one of those gaps was filled by third parties, unevenly.

The pre-training changes are incremental: two trillion tokens rather than one to 1.4, a 4k context, grouped-query attention at the largest size. The post-training is the contribution. Supervised fine-tuning used a deliberately small set of high-quality human-written examples — 27,540 in the end — after the authors found that their own vendor-annotated data beat millions of examples drawn from third-party instruction sets. Preference data was then collected over successive rounds, each on the current model's own outputs, so the reward signal tracked the policy rather than a stale one.

Two reward models were trained, one for helpfulness and one for safety, so that the safety objective does not simply tax helpfulness through a single blended score. Optimisation combined rejection sampling with PPO, and a mechanism the paper calls Ghost Attention was added to stop system-level instructions from decaying over a long conversation.

Llama 3 scaled the same shape — around fifteen trillion tokens, a larger tokenizer vocabulary, grouped-query attention at every size, a 405B model — and replaced PPO with rejection sampling plus direct preference optimisation, which is markedly more stable to run.

An open-weight chat model with a commercial licence reset what the ecosystem expected as a starting point. Llama became the substrate: the shape that inference servers optimised for, that quantisation formats targeted, and that adapter tooling assumed by default.

The costs are worth stating without flinching. Safety tuning produced measurable over-refusal on benign prompts, and the community removed it within days through further fine-tuning — which is the durable lesson that **alignment held in weights is not a property of a model whose weights you have given away**. The licence is open-weight, not open-source: an acceptable-use policy governs deployment and a monthly-active-user threshold carves out the largest competitors.

And the transparency ran backwards. LLaMA-1 listed its corpora and their token proportions, and that reproducibility was the argument for releasing it at all. Llama-2 and Llama-3 describe their data only in general terms. The lineage became more useful and less inspectable at the same time.

refs.t: Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models
The Llama 3 Herd of Models
LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models

gpt3>llama.lead: GPT-3 established that a sufficiently large language model acquires tasks from examples in its prompt, with no gradient updates at all. It simultaneously established that you would only ever meet such a model through a metered API. LLaMA's argument was that the first result did not require the second: the same behaviour was reachable at a fraction of the parameters, on entirely public data, with the weights written to disk.

blocks.b:
The finding was that scale changes the interface. A 175-billion-parameter model given a task description and a handful of examples performs the task, and performance improves with the number of examples supplied in the context. Fine-tuning stopped being the only way to specify what you wanted.

The result rested on a scaling argument that later turned out to be miscalibrated. The scaling laws then available suggested that when compute increases, most of the increase should be spent on parameters rather than on data, and GPT-3's 175 billion parameters trained on a few hundred billion tokens follows that allocation directly.

For everyone outside the lab, the consequence was that the object of study became a rate-limited endpoint that could be changed or withdrawn without notice. Ablation was impossible, reproduction was impossible, and the model's own weights were an expense to be paid on every token served, forever.

LLaMA accepted the capability finding and rejected the allocation. Chinchilla had already shown, by fitting loss as

$L(N, D) = E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}}$

where $N$ is parameter count and $D$ training tokens, that the two exponents are close enough that a fixed compute budget should grow $N$ and $D$ together. Under that fit GPT-3 was badly undertrained for its size.

LLaMA went past even the compute-optimal point, and for a reason that has nothing to do with training. Training is paid once; inference is paid on every request. So a 7B model trained on a trillion tokens is a worse use of training compute and a far better model to own. The data was public throughout — web crawl, code, Wikipedia, arXiv, StackExchange, books — described precisely enough to be re-collected.

The architecture was borrowed rather than invented: RMSNorm pre-normalisation, SwiGLU, rotary embeddings. The paper reported the 13B model ahead of GPT-3 on most benchmarks.

The open-weight ecosystem appeared essentially in one step. Within weeks there were instruction-tuned derivatives, CPU runtimes that ran the smaller models on laptops, quantisation formats and low-rank adapters — all of which required only that someone, once, release weights small enough to work with. Parameter count stopped being the headline figure, and tokens-per-parameter became the number people argued about.

The costs run in two directions. Training well past compute-optimal makes each base model substantially more expensive to produce, so base-model training concentrated further into a few well-capitalised labs even as their outputs were shared more widely. The release mechanism — an application form for researchers — failed within a week, meaning the de facto distribution policy was set by a leak rather than by a decision.

And the openness was one-directional: weights without training code, without the data itself, and without any means of reproducing the run that produced them.

refs.t: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models

mixtral>llama2.lead: This arrow is not descent, and it would be dishonest to draw it as one. Mixtral and the Llama-2/3 line are two answers, released within months of each other, to a single question: where the next factor of quality per unit of serving cost comes from. Their genuine shared ancestry runs back through LLaMA, not between them — Mistral's decoder is a Llama-shaped decoder — and what separates them is a bet about which resource is scarce.

blocks.b:
The sparse bet is that arithmetic is the scarce resource and memory is not. Mixtral holds around 47 billion parameters and activates roughly 13 for any given token, and its authors reported it matching or beating a 70-billion-parameter dense Llama across most benchmarks they evaluated. The weights came under Apache 2.0, with no acceptable-use policy and no user-count threshold attached.

The reasoning behind it is a serving argument. In a datacentre running large batches, throughput is bounded by floating-point operations; memory is comparatively cheap and, once the model fits within one node, expert routing costs nothing that crosses the network. Under those conditions sparsity is close to free quality: you buy the representational capacity of a large model and pay the arithmetic of a small one.

The premise it depends on is the batch. Every expert needs work for the saving to materialise.

blocks.h: What the Llama line bet on
blocks.b:
The dense bet is that memory and tooling are the scarce resources and arithmetic is affordable. Every parameter is active for every token, and quality is bought instead with training tokens and post-training effort — Llama 3 trained on roughly fifteen trillion tokens is far past compute-optimal by deliberate choice, and ships with preference tuning already applied.

The 8B model exists because of what a dense 8B can do outside a datacentre. It quantises to four bits and runs on a laptop with predictable degradation. It fine-tunes with low-rank adapters on a single GPU. It behaves identically in every serving stack because there is no routing to get wrong, no capacity factor to tune, and no dependency on how a batch happens to be composed.

For the enormous population of users whose constraint is one GPU rather than one cluster, this is the whole argument, and Mixtral's active-parameter advantage buys them nothing at all.

It settled by splitting, which is the honest ending. At small scale and for local deployment, dense won on ergonomics: quantisation formats, adapter libraries and inference runtimes all grew around Llama-shaped decoders, and Llama-3-70B closed most of the quality gap that Mixtral had opened while remaining a single dense checkpoint people could handle.

At the frontier the sparse bet won outright. The large open models that followed — DeepSeek's V2 and V3 line, Qwen's mixture models, and eventually Meta's own Llama 4 — are mixtures of experts, because at datacentre batch sizes the arithmetic saving is real, memory is the cheaper resource to buy, and total capacity is what determines quality.

The two positions were never actually in contradiction. They were priced for different deployment regimes, and the cost of treating them as rivals was several years of benchmark comparisons that quietly held the wrong quantity fixed — active parameters or resident parameters, depending on which side was publishing.

instructgpt>dpo.lead: InstructGPT's alignment stage kept four models in flight — a policy, a frozen reference, a learned reward model and a value network — and trained them with PPO. DPO showed the reward model was never structurally necessary: the KL-constrained objective InstructGPT maximised has a closed-form optimum, and reading that optimum backwards expresses the reward in terms of the policy itself.

blocks.b:
Ouyang et al. collected human comparisons between sampled outputs, fitted a Bradley–Terry reward model $r_\phi$ to them, then optimised the policy against that surrogate under a penalty for drifting from the supervised model:

$$\max_{\pi}\; \mathbb{E}_{x,\,y\sim\pi}\big[r_\phi(x,y)\big] \;-\; \beta\,\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\big[\pi(y\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)\big]$$

The payoff settled the argument: labellers preferred the 1.3B InstructGPT's outputs to those of the 175B GPT-3, a model over a hundred times its size. The cost was the machinery. Training needed fresh on-policy samples inside the loop, a value network for PPO's advantage estimates, and clipping and KL coefficients that were known to be temperamental. And because $r_\phi$ is a surrogate fitted on finitely many comparisons, the policy could find outputs it scored highly and humans did not — reward hacking, which the KL term restrains rather than prevents.

The maximiser of that objective is known in closed form:

$$\pi^{*}(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{Z(x)}\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp\!\big(r(x,y)/\beta\big)$$

Rafailov et al. solved it for the reward rather than the policy, giving $r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi^{*}(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)}+\beta\log Z(x)$. Substituted into the Bradley–Terry likelihood the intractable $Z(x)$ **cancels**, because both responses in a preference pair share a prompt. What survives is an ordinary supervised loss on preference data:

$$-\log\sigma\!\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w\mid x)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}\right)$$

Kept: the Bradley–Terry model of preference, the reference policy, and $\beta$ as the same KL knob it always was. Discarded: the reward model, the rollouts, the value network, the clipping. Added: a second frozen forward pass, and nothing else.

Post-training stopped requiring a distributed RL stack. A preference set, two forward passes and a cross-entropy loss run on the same code that does supervised fine-tuning, which is why open post-training recipes adopted DPO almost immediately.

The loss is paid in being wholly offline. PPO resampled from the current policy, so the reward model was queried where the policy actually was; DPO sees only a fixed set of pairs, and its implicit reward is unconstrained away from them. Practitioners observed the log-probability of chosen and rejected responses both falling, the margin widening while neither response becomes more likely. Removing the explicit reward model leaves only the policy's implicit reward, $\beta\log(\pi_\theta/\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})$, to do what a separate one did — best-of-$n$ reranking, filtering, scoring at inference — and it is a poorer scorer away from the pairs it was fitted on. Much of the follow-up work (IPO, KTO, ORPO, SimPO, and iterative or online DPO) is an attempt to recover one of those two losses without reinstating PPO.
