Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model

transformer>ldm.lead: Little of the Transformer's architecture survives into Stable Diffusion's backbone, which is a convolutional U-Net with whole Transformer blocks — self-attention, cross-attention, LayerNorm and a feedforward — spliced in at several resolutions. What crossed over is cross-attention — the encoder–decoder mechanism by which one sequence reads another — and it arrived priced at the number of image positions times the number of text tokens, on top of a self-attention that is quadratic in image positions, which is part of why the diffusion had to move into a latent space at all.

blocks.b:
The Transformer's encoder–decoder attention computes

$$\mathrm{Attn}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V$$

where the queries $Q$ come from one set of positions and the keys and values $K,V$ from another. Nothing in that expression requires the two sets to have the same length, the same ordering, or the same origin: it is a differentiable lookup from an arbitrary query set into an arbitrary key–value memory, with the correspondence learned rather than specified. In 2017 that generality was used only to let a decoder read a source sentence. It also fixes the price. The cost is proportional to the product of the two set sizes, so the mechanism is affordable when the query set is a sentence and unaffordable when it is a grid of pixels.

blocks.h: What Stable Diffusion did with it
blocks.b:
Rombach et al. kept the layer and discarded the architecture around it. The backbone stays a convolutional U-Net, which supplies locality and translation equivariance for free and needs no positional encodings, and cross-attention blocks are inserted at the coarser resolutions. A conditioning encoder $\tau_\theta$ turns a prompt into a token sequence; the U-Net's spatial feature map is flattened into queries, and $K$ and $V$ are projections of $\tau_\theta(y)$.

The removal only works because of the autoencoder. A $512\times512$ image is over 260,000 query positions, which the quadratic term makes hopeless; compressed by a factor of eight, the latent grid is $64\times64$, about 4,000 positions, and both self- and cross-attention become routine. **The latent space is not only a compute saving on diffusion — it is what makes the borrowed mechanism usable.**

Conditioning became modular. Because $\tau_\theta$ is only required to emit a sequence of vectors, the same trained U-Net accepts text, class labels, layouts, or another image, and the text encoder can be swapped without touching the generator — which is exactly what later models did, moving from BERT-style encoders to CLIP and then to combinations of CLIP and T5. Text-to-image generation ran on consumer GPUs, and the weights were released, so the derivative ecosystem is largely built on this one design.

Two costs followed. Attention over a prompt binds concepts by similarity, with no compositional guarantee, so attribute binding, counting and negation fail in characteristic ways. And the autoencoder that made the attention affordable discards high-frequency detail: small faces and rendered text are where the reconstruction error shows first.

refs.t: Attention Is All You Need
High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models

transformer>dt.lead: Decision Transformer borrows no mechanism from the Transformer that needed adapting; it borrows the architecture unchanged and instead changes what reinforcement learning is taken to be. An offline dataset of trajectories is treated as a corpus, and control becomes next-token prediction with the return written into the context.

blocks.b:
A causal decoder models a joint distribution over an arbitrary token sequence by factorising it autoregressively, and every position can read every earlier position in one attention step. That second property is the one that matters here. Temporal-difference learning propagates value information one bootstrap at a time, so credit for an action taken a thousand steps before the reward arrives has to survive a thousand noisy backups — and off-policy bootstrapping with function approximation is precisely the combination known to diverge.

A Transformer trained by maximum likelihood has neither problem, because it never bootstraps. It also inherits the scaling behaviour of language modelling: the same block, the same optimiser, the same relationship between capacity, data and loss. Chen et al. needed only to decide what a token should be.

A trajectory is written as $(\hat{R}_1, s_1, a_1, \hat{R}_2, s_2, a_2, \ldots)$, where $\hat{R}_t=\sum_{t'\ge t} r_{t'}$ is the **return-to-go**: not the reward just received but the total still to come. Each modality gets its own embedding, a timestep encoding is added, and a GPT is trained to predict the action token by ordinary supervised loss.

Thrown away: the value function, the Bellman backup, the policy-improvement step, the target networks, the discount factor. What had to be added to make the removal survive is the return conditioning. Without it the model is behaviour cloning and inherits the average quality of the data; with it, one asks at test time for a high return and the model completes the trajectory that would have produced it. The idea has antecedents in upside-down RL and reward-conditioned policies, which Chen et al. acknowledge; the contribution is doing it with a sequence model at scale.

blocks.h: What it bought and what it cost
blocks.b:
It made offline RL a place where language-model infrastructure applies directly, and the concurrent Trajectory Transformer, then Gato and multi-game agents, followed the same route. On long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks where TD methods struggle to assign credit, conditional sequence modelling was competitive without a single stability trick.

The cost is stitching. Dynamic programming can compose the good first half of one trajectory with the good second half of another and produce a policy better than anything in the data; return-conditioned supervised learning cannot, because it only ever imitates completions it has seen. Subsequent analysis showed the approach also needs near-deterministic dynamics — under stochastic transitions, a high observed return may reflect luck rather than a good action, and conditioning on it asks the model to reproduce the luck.

refs.t: Decision Transformer: Reinforcement Learning via Sequence Modeling
Offline Reinforcement Learning as One Big Sequence Modeling Problem

lstm>showtell.lead: Show and Tell is the cleanest instance of a join several groups made at once in 2014: a convolutional recogniser trained on ImageNet wired to a gated recurrent decoder built for machine translation, alongside m-RNN, LRCN and Karpathy and Fei-Fei's alignment model. The LSTM contributed a generator that can be handed an arbitrary initial state and asked to emit a sentence, and the image was inserted as that state.

blocks.b:
The cell state updates additively — by 2014 in the form $c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot g_t$, the forget gate having been added by Gers et al. in 2000 to Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's original carousel — so information injected early passes forward through elementwise gating rather than through repeated multiplication by a recurrent Jacobian. That is what allows a conditioning signal supplied at step zero to still be influencing the output twenty words later, where a plain RNN would have lost it.

By 2014 that property had been turned into a template. Sutskever et al. encoded a source sentence into a fixed vector with one LSTM and decoded the translation with another, showing that a trained LSTM decoder is essentially a language model with a settable initial condition. The encoder's identity was never load-bearing — only the fact that it produced a vector of the right size.

Vinyals et al. took the translation model and replaced the source-language encoder with a convolutional network, maximising

$$\log p(S\mid I)=\sum_{t}\log p(S_t \mid I, S_0,\ldots,S_{t-1})$$

The image enters exactly once, as a linear projection of the CNN's penultimate activations fed in at position $-1$, before the first word embedding. Feeding it at every step was tried and was worse — the model overfits the visual signal.

What had to be added was care about gradients. The CNN was pretrained and initially held fixed, because the noisy gradients from a randomly initialised decoder would otherwise destroy representations that took far more data to learn than the captioning corpus contains. On the Pascal sentence set, BLEU-1 rose from around 25 for the previous best system to 59, against roughly 69 for humans.

blocks.h: What followed, and what the metric hid
blocks.b:
The pattern — frozen visual encoder, projection into the token stream of a language model, train the join — is the direct ancestor of every later captioning and visual-dialogue system, and survives essentially unchanged in modern vision-language models where the decoder is a Transformer rather than an LSTM.

Its weakness was visible within a year. A single vector at step zero is the same fixed-size bottleneck that Bahdanau had just diagnosed in translation, and Show, Attend and Tell replaced it with attention over a spatial feature grid. The evaluation was weaker still: contemporaneous work showed that a nearest-neighbour baseline, retrieving a caption from the training set, scored competitively on BLEU, which says the metric was largely rewarding fluent dataset-typical phrasing rather than accurate description.

refs.t: Show and Tell: A Neural Image Caption Generator
Show, Attend and Tell: Neural Image Caption Generation with Visual Attention
Long Short-Term Memory

bert>vilbert.lead: ViLBERT and LXMERT are BERT's recipe applied to a second modality: the same Transformer stack, the same masked-denoising pretraining, the same pretrain-then-fine-tune deployment, with images admitted as sequences of detected object regions. The transfer was mostly clean, and where it was not — visual tokens are not discrete — is where the interesting engineering sits.

blocks.b:
Masked language modelling removed the constraint that a pretraining objective must factorise autoregressively. Corrupt a fraction of the tokens, ask a bidirectional encoder to recover them, and every position is trained with context from both sides, at a cost of only the masked fraction per pass. The signal is free: any corpus of coherent context supplies it.

Two further pieces of the recipe travelled. Next-sentence prediction showed a paired-sequence objective, in which the model judges whether two segments genuinely belong together, could be stacked on top of the token-level one. And the fine-tuning protocol — keep the encoder, attach a small head, tune the whole thing on a modest labelled set — turned pretraining into infrastructure rather than a single result.

An image was represented as a set of regions from a Faster R-CNN detector, each a pooled feature vector plus its box geometry, and treated as tokens. Masked language modelling carried over unaltered; the pair objective became image–text alignment, predicting whether a caption belongs to an image.

The masked-region objective is where the analogy breaks. There is no vocabulary to softmax over, so masked regions are supervised by regressing the feature or by matching the detector's predicted class distribution — a weaker signal than recovering a discrete token, and one whose ceiling is the detector's own accuracy. ViLBERT also declined to use a single stack, arguing that a much richer text side would dominate a shared one; it runs two streams joined by co-attention layers that exchange keys and values, and LXMERT reaches the same shape with separate encoders under a cross-modality encoder.

blocks.h: What followed, and the detector's price
blocks.b:
Vision-language pretraining became a standard stage, and downstream tasks — VQA, referring expressions, retrieval — stopped being separately engineered architectures and became heads on a pretrained encoder.

The cost was the detector. Everything the model can ground is bounded by a fixed object vocabulary of roughly 1,600 Visual Genome classes; anything outside a box, including most of the scene's texture and layout, is discarded before the Transformer sees it; and detection dominates inference time. Later work removed it in two directions. ViLT dropped regions for linear patch embeddings, showing most of the accuracy survived. CLIP dropped the cross-modal attention entirely, replacing careful fusion and small curated corpora with a contrastive objective over web-scale pairs, and beat the two-stream models on transfer.

refs.t: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
ViLBERT: Pretraining Task-Agnostic Visiolinguistic Representations
LXMERT: Learning Cross-Modality Encoder Representations from Transformers

transformer>clip.lead: CLIP is a Transformer text encoder and a vision backbone joined by a contrastive objective, and the merge is what makes it work. The Transformer supplies an encoder that turns arbitrary natural language into a vector, which is what dissolves the fixed label set; the contrastive loss supplies a training signal cheap enough to consume four hundred million web image–text pairs.

blocks.h: Text as a vector, not an index
blocks.b:
A classifier's output layer is an index into a fixed taxonomy: ImageNet's thousand classes are a thousand rows of a matrix, and a class outside them cannot be named. A Transformer encoder replaces the index with a computed embedding of a string. CLIP's text tower is small by language-model standards — twelve layers, 512 wide, byte-pair encoded, with the final token's activations layer-normed and projected — but its output lives in the same space as the image embedding, so classification becomes nearest-neighbour search among embedded sentences.

The Transformer contributed the image side too. With ViT, patches are tokens and the same block serves both modalities, so the two towers differ mainly in their input embedding — a uniformity that later made joint scaling straightforward.

blocks.h: The objective that made scale affordable
blocks.b:
Radford et al. first tried predicting the caption. Generation is a demanding target — the model must get word order and phrasing right, not just content — and it was slow to reach useful zero-shot accuracy; predicting a bag of words instead was several times more efficient, and replacing prediction with a contrastive objective gained several times again.

What remains is a batch of $N$ pairs, cosine similarities between all $N^2$ combinations scaled by a learned temperature, and a symmetric cross-entropy that identifies the true pairing along rows and columns. **The two towers never attend to each other** — unlike ViLBERT, the only interaction is a dot product — so the $N^2$ comparisons cost one matrix multiplication rather than $N^2$ forward passes, and embeddings can be precomputed and cached.

Zero-shot ImageNet accuracy matched a ResNet-50 trained on ImageNet itself, and robustness to distribution shift was markedly better than for models fitted to a single label set. Prompt wording mattered enough that templating and ensembling were worth nearly five points. CLIP embeddings then became infrastructure: the text conditioner in diffusion models, the vision encoder in multimodal language models, the filter used to assemble later web datasets.

The cost is written into the objective. All it demands is that a caption's vector be closer to its image than to others in the batch, and unordered word content usually suffices to win that contest. So CLIP behaves substantially like a bag of concepts: word order, spatial relations, counting and negation are weakly represented, and diagnostic benchmarks built on swapped-word captions expose it directly.

refs.t: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale

t5>imagen.lead: Imagen takes a T5 encoder trained only on text, freezes it, and uses its output as the conditioning signal for a diffusion model. The transfer is unusually literal — no fine-tuning, no gradient into the encoder — and the paper's central finding is about that choice: enlarging the frozen language encoder improved image–text alignment and sample fidelity more than enlarging the diffusion model did.

blocks.h: What T5 left behind for others to use
blocks.b:
The text-to-text framing is not what Imagen needed. What it needed was the by-product: a family of large encoders trained on a very large, very varied crawl of ordinary written English, released publicly, at several sizes along the same recipe.

That corpus is the point. The alternative conditioning signal available in 2022 was a CLIP text encoder, trained on alt-text — short, formulaic, and written to accompany rather than describe. A T5 encoder has seen syntax that alt-text does not contain: subordination, negation, relative clauses, extended modification. And because the checkpoints came in a size ladder from small to eleven billion parameters, the question of how much the encoder matters could be answered by ablation rather than argument.

blocks.h: Freezing it, and what that forced
blocks.b:
Saharia et al. condition a $64\times64$ diffusion model on the frozen encoder's token embeddings by cross-attention, then upsample twice with further diffusion models. Freezing buys a great deal: text embeddings are computed once, offline, so the encoder contributes nothing to training cost and cannot be degraded by image gradients.

What had to be added was a way to survive the guidance the alignment then demanded. Classifier-free guidance extrapolates between conditional and unconditional predictions, and at the large weights that give faithful prompt-following it drives the predicted image outside the valid pixel range, producing saturated, washed-out samples. **Dynamic thresholding** fixes it: at each step, take a high percentile of the absolute values in the predicted clean image, clip to that threshold, and rescale by it, so the range is enforced adaptively rather than by a fixed clamp.

blocks.h: What it settled, and what it did not
blocks.b:
The frozen unimodal encoder became a standard component. Later open text-to-image systems adopted T5-XXL, alone or alongside CLIP encoders, extending Imagen's finding that a text-only encoder wins on prompt alignment; the case for running both came later, from eDiff-I onwards, that two encoders see different distributions of language and fail differently. The result also reframed where capacity should go, away from the generator and towards the conditioning.

The bill is paid in memory and in what language modelling cannot teach. A multi-billion-parameter encoder that never learns anything from images occupies a large share of the budget, and text pretraining alone does not confer grounded understanding of quantity, spatial arrangement, or which adjective attaches to which noun — the failures DrawBench was built to probe. Imagen itself was never released, so its influence runs through reimplementations rather than its weights.

refs.t: Photorealistic Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Deep Language Understanding
Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer

transformer>longformer.lead: The Transformer's cost is one object: an $n \times n$ score matrix in which every query meets every key. Longformer's claim is that most of that matrix is dead weight, because trained attention concentrates locally, and that a fixed pattern of sliding windows plus a handful of full-attention tokens recovers what the dense matrix was doing at a cost linear in length.

blocks.b:
The Transformer's advantage over recurrence was path length: any position reaches any other within one layer. The mechanism materialises the scores $QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$ and the probabilities that follow — two $n \times n$ tensors per head per layer, retained through the backward pass. At BERT's 512 tokens that is affordable; at a few thousand it dominates memory, so long documents were handled by chunking and stitching, which restores the very boundary attention had removed. A question at token 3000 could not see its evidence at token 200.

Two observations made a sparse replacement plausible. Attention distributions in trained models are mostly **peaked and local**, so the great majority of entries contribute almost nothing; and stacking layers compounds receptive field as it does in a convolutional network, so one-hop reach is not needed in every layer for long-range information to be available in the stack.

Longformer leaves dot-product softmax attention untouched and changes only which pairs are scored. Each token attends to a band of $w$ neighbours, giving $O(nw)$, and dilating the band in the upper layers widens the reach without extra computation. Compatibility is kept deliberately: the model initialises from RoBERTa and copies its 512 position embeddings repeatedly out to 4096 rather than pretraining a long-context encoder from scratch.

What had to be added is an escape hatch, because pure windows cannot aggregate — a classification token, or the question tokens in extractive QA, must see everything. Selected positions are therefore given global attention in both directions, with their own projection matrices, so the global and local roles need not share parameters. And a banded score matrix is not a dense matrix multiplication, so the saving is realised only through a custom kernel.

blocks.h: What it made possible, and the bill
blocks.b:
Documents stopped being chunked. Longformer handled WikiHop, TriviaQA and long-document classification without sliding-window ensembling, and its encoder-decoder variant reached summarisation at arXiv-paper length. The template — a local band plus a few global tokens — reappears in BigBird, in windowed vision transformers, and in most long-context adaptation recipes since.

Two costs. The pattern is a prior fixed by hand: which tokens are global is a per-task judgement, and a task whose evidence is diffuse gets no help from a window. And the asymptotic saving converts poorly into wall-clock time, because banded multiplication uses the hardware worse than dense multiplication does — the observation FlashAttention would later turn against the sparse-attention programme as a whole. Distant positions now communicate only through intermediate layers, so depth rather than a single hop carries long-range information, which is the property the Transformer had been valued for removing.

refs.t: Attention Is All You Need
Longformer: The Long-Document Transformer
Big Bird: Transformers for Longer Sequences

longformer>performer.lead: These are siblings rather than parent and child: Longformer, Linformer and Performer all appeared within months of each other in 2020, and none derives from the others. What the arrow records is a change of premise. Longformer deletes entries from the attention matrix according to a pattern fixed in advance; the linear-attention line declines to build the matrix at all, on the grounds that it is either low rank or a kernel in disguise.

blocks.b:
Longformer's argument is empirical: attention mass in trained models is mostly local, so zeroing most of the matrix loses little. That buys $O(nw)$ but concedes two things. The support of the pattern is chosen by the designer rather than learned, so an interaction it excludes is unavailable at that layer however important it turns out to be; and the computation inside the band is still dense, which is why the method needs a hand-written banded kernel before it is fast at all.

By posing the problem as which entries to keep, Longformer also framed the question its contemporaries answered differently. If the $n \times n$ matrix is what makes attention expensive, sparsity is only one way to avoid it. The alternative is to let every pair interact in principle while never forming the object that represents those interactions — an assumption about the matrix's structure rather than its support.

blocks.h: Two ways not to build it
blocks.b:
Linformer assumes the softmax matrix is approximately low rank — supported by the spectrum measured in trained models and a Johnson–Lindenstrauss style bound — and projects keys and values down the sequence axis with learned matrices, giving cost linear in $n$ for a fixed projection width. Performer assumes instead that softmax is a kernel and that **a kernel has a feature map**: for a random map $\phi$ with $\mathbb{E}[\phi(q)^\top \phi(k)] \approx \exp(q^\top k/\sqrt{d})$, associativity does the rest.

$\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top)V \approx \hat{D}^{-1}\big(\phi(Q)\,(\phi(K)^\top V)\big)$

Contracting the length axis first means nothing of size $n \times n$ ever exists. Both discard the hand-designed pattern, and both must add something to make the removal survivable. Performer's features have to be positive rather than trigonometric, or the estimator's variance becomes unusable exactly where the softmax is sharp. Linformer's projections are tied to a fixed sequence length and mix positions along the sequence, which breaks causal masking outright.

The outcome was a taxonomy rather than a winner. Long Range Arena arrived the same year to compare these methods on common tasks, and it made the trade legible: linear methods are cheap and stable, and weaker wherever a task needs a precise lookup.

That failure mode follows from the assumptions themselves. A near-one-hot attention row is a sharp, high-rank object, which is precisely what a rank-$k$ projection or a finite random-feature estimate approximates worst, so the degradation lands on retrieval, copying and induction — the behaviours that make attention worth having in a language model. Linear attention persisted where sequences are long and dependencies diffuse, and in deployments with hard efficiency budgets, but not in frontier language models. By 2022 the question had changed from how best to approximate attention to whether it needed approximating at all.

refs.t: Linformer: Self-Attention with Linear Complexity
Rethinking Attention with Performers
Long Range Arena: A Benchmark for Efficient Transformers

performer>flashattn.lead: The linear-attention line traded accuracy for asymptotics: fewer floating-point operations, an approximate softmax. FlashAttention is the reply that the trade was unnecessary, because operations were never the binding constraint — attention on a GPU is limited by traffic to memory. The same refusal to materialise the score matrix can be had exactly rather than approximately.

blocks.b:
Performer's lasting contribution is less its estimator than its extension of an existing move to softmax itself: the linear-attention line had already shown that reordering the contraction lets the score matrix go unbuilt, and Performer showed the same could be had for the softmax kernel — the refusal to materialise, not the mechanism, is what FlashAttention keeps. That decoupling is what FlashAttention keeps.

The other bequest was negative and took two years to become plain. Across Long Range Arena and in language-model practice, approximate attention held up where dependencies were diffuse and gave way where recall had to be precise, and its advantage in floating-point operations frequently failed to appear as an advantage in wall-clock time. Replacing one large fused matrix multiplication with several small memory-bound ones can cost more than it saves. Once **the quantity being optimised was seen to be the wrong quantity**, an exact method became worth attempting rather than obviously hopeless.

A modern accelerator pairs tens of gigabytes of high-bandwidth memory with a much smaller and far faster on-chip SRAM. A textbook attention kernel writes the scores to HBM, reads them back to normalise, writes the probabilities, then reads them again to multiply by $V$ — several round trips of $n \times n$ data for an operation of low arithmetic intensity.

FlashAttention tiles $Q$, $K$ and $V$ into blocks that fit on chip and accumulates the softmax online, carrying a running maximum $m$ and normaliser $\ell$ and rescaling the partial output whenever a new block raises the maximum:

$\ell^{\mathrm{new}} = e^{m^{\mathrm{old}} - m^{\mathrm{new}}}\ell^{\mathrm{old}} + e^{\tilde{m} - m^{\mathrm{new}}}\tilde{\ell}$

Nothing is approximated. The backward pass, which needs the probabilities, recomputes them from the saved row statistics rather than storing them — spending arithmetic, which is abundant, to save memory traffic, which is not.

Attention's memory became linear in sequence length and throughput rose several-fold at GPT-2 scale, and a Transformer running on it cleared Path-X at sixteen thousand tokens — a task on which every model Long Range Arena had tested, exact and approximate alike, sat at chance. Almost all frontier long-context training since runs on FlashAttention or a descendant, and most of the efficient-attention literature that preceded it stopped being deployed.

The costs are worth stating plainly. The method is still quadratic in arithmetic; it moved the constant and the memory, not the exponent, so the wall returns at long enough context. And it relocated progress into the kernel. A tiling schedule tuned to one generation's on-chip budget must be rewritten for the next, and an architectural idea that cannot be expressed as a fused kernel now loses on wall-clock to one that can, whatever its complexity class promises.

refs.t: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
Online normalizer calculation for softmax
Rethinking Attention with Performers

transformer>flashattn.lead: This is the rarest kind of successor: one that changes nothing about the model. FlashAttention computes precisely the function defined in 2017 — same parameters, same outputs up to floating-point reassociation — and alters only how that computation is scheduled against the memory hierarchy. What it removes is not a limitation of the Transformer but an assumption in every implementation of it.

blocks.b:
Vaswani et al. chose attention partly for hardware reasons: dense matrix multiplication, parallel across positions, no sequential loop. The instinct was right at the wrong granularity. The definition

$\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$

names two intermediate tensors, the scores and the probabilities, each $n \times n$ per head per layer, and every implementation stored both. In training they must also be kept for the backward pass, so activation memory — not parameter count, not arithmetic — set the sequence length a given accelerator could train on. Quadratic cost was consequently read as a property of attention itself. **In arithmetic it is; in memory it is not.** The output is an $n \times d$ object and can be produced without the square ones ever existing, which is a fact about the schedule rather than about the model.

Everything defining the model is kept, which is why a checkpoint trained with a standard kernel runs unchanged under this one: the same projections, the same softmax, the same numerics up to summation order. What is thrown away is the materialised matrix. Queries, keys and values are tiled into blocks small enough for on-chip SRAM, the softmax is accumulated blockwise with running maxima and normalisers, and the partial output is rescaled as each block arrives.

To make the removal work, the backward pass must recompute the probabilities it no longer holds, from the stored row statistics and the same tiling. That is extra arithmetic bought with far fewer trips to high-bandwidth memory, and the exchange is favourable because attention's arithmetic intensity is low — the kernel spends most of its time waiting on memory rather than computing. The footprint becomes linear in sequence length while the arithmetic stays quadratic.

The visible result was speed, roughly threefold on GPT-2 training with a smaller but real end-to-end gain at BERT scale. The structural result was context length: sequences that could not be trained because their activations would not fit became merely expensive, and the move from two-thousand-token to hundred-thousand-token contexts owes more to this kernel and its successors than to any change of architecture.

Two costs followed. The bottleneck moved rather than disappeared — with training activations linear, autoregressive inference is now limited by the KV cache, which grows with context and batch and motivated multi-query and grouped-query attention, paged caches, and the state-space alternatives. And the Transformer became partly a hardware artefact: its lead now includes years of kernel engineering that a challenger does not inherit, so a replacement has to be better by more than its idea.

s4>mamba.lead: S4 showed that a linear state-space model, given the right initialisation and the right algebra, could carry information across tens of thousands of steps and still be trained in parallel as a convolution. Mamba changes one word in that description: the dynamics stop being fixed and become functions of the input. Everything difficult about Mamba follows from the fact that this makes the convolution impossible.

blocks.b:
S4 discretises a continuous linear system, $x'(t) = Ax(t) + Bu(t)$ with $y(t) = Cx(t)$, into a linear recurrence, then observes that a fixed linear recurrence unrolls into a convolution whose kernel is $(\bar{C}\bar{B},\, \bar{C}\bar{A}\bar{B},\, \dots)$. Two things make that usable. HiPPO supplies a structured $A$ under which the state is an optimal running polynomial summary of the input's history; randomly initialised state matrices do markedly worse, and the ablation is unambiguous. And a normal-plus-low-rank parameterisation lets the whole kernel be computed in $O(n\log n)$ rather than unrolled step by step. The payoff was Path-X, a sixteen-thousand-step task on which every efficient Transformer tested had sat at chance.

All of this rests on time-invariance: $A$, $B$ and $C$ do not depend on position, which is exactly what makes the recurrence a convolution.

Gu and Dao isolated the resulting weakness with two synthetic tasks. Selective copying requires ignoring a variable amount of filler; induction heads require retrieving whatever followed a token seen earlier. Both need the model to **decide from content what to keep**, and a time-invariant system cannot: its kernel is the same whatever arrives.

Mamba makes the step size $\Delta$ and the maps $B$ and $C$ functions of the current input, so the dynamics vary per position. In the discretisation $\bar{A} = \exp(\Delta A)$, a large $\Delta$ pulls the state towards the current token and a small one holds the state and ignores it — the forget gate of an LSTM recovered as a limit of a continuous system. The convolution is now gone, so training uses a parallel associative scan rather than an FFT, with the expanded state held in SRAM, discretisation fused into the scan, and activations recomputed in the backward pass: FlashAttention's method transplanted.

Selectivity is what carried state-space models out of audio, time series and synthetic long-range tasks and into language modelling. Mamba matched Transformer baselines of substantially larger parameter count at the scales its authors could train, with constant memory per generated token and no KV cache at all.

Two things were surrendered. HiPPO's optimality argument is a statement about a time-invariant system, so once the dynamics vary the initialisation becomes heuristic rather than derived — the theory that motivated S4 no longer covers its successor. And selection changes what is stored, not how much: the state is still fixed in size, so exact recall from long context remains weaker than attention's. That is why serious deployments are mostly hybrids that retain a few attention layers, and why Mamba-2's reframing of the selective SSM as a form of structured masked attention mattered as much for tooling as for theory.

transformer>mamba.lead: Mamba is not a Transformer variant; it replaces the sequence mixer outright and keeps nearly everything else the Transformer established. The contrast is best put as memory: attention retains every token it has seen and pays for that at every step, while a selective state-space model compresses the past into a state of fixed size and pays a constant. Neither choice is free, and the difference is not efficiency but what can be remembered.

blocks.b:
Attention's defining property is that **its representation of the past is the past**: keys and values are retained for every previous token, and any one of them can be recovered exactly by a query that matches it. In training that costs quadratic arithmetic. In generation it costs the KV cache, which grows with context length and batch size and must be read in full for every token emitted, making decoding memory-bandwidth-bound.

No kernel removes this. FlashAttention made training activations linear and left the cache untouched; multi-query and grouped-query attention, paged caches and cache quantisation all shrink a structure the design implies rather than eliminating it. The Transformer buys lossless access to arbitrary past content and pays for it at every step, indefinitely.

A selective state-space model holds a state of fixed size and updates it once per token, so generation costs the same at position ten and at position a hundred thousand, and there is nothing to cache. What Mamba gives up is verbatim storage: nothing survives from the past except through a running summary, and the input-dependent gating decides what enters it.

Making that competitive required adding selection, which earlier state-space models lacked, and a hardware-aware scan, because content-dependent dynamics forfeit the convolution that made S4 trainable in parallel. Almost everything else is inherited from the incumbent — the residual pre-norm stack, the alternation of a sequence mixer with a position-wise MLP, the tokeniser and training recipe, the practice of validating a mixer by matched-compute scaling comparison, and the kernel discipline FlashAttention established. The competition is over one component, not the paradigm.

The evidence so far is legible rather than settled. Mamba matched Transformer baselines of considerably larger size at the scales its authors trained, and it is strongest where inputs are long, dense and continuous — audio waveforms, genomic sequences, high-rate signals — which is where attention has always been worst. It is weakest where a task requires copying a span or retrieving a specific fact from context, a limit that follows from the capacity of a fixed state rather than from insufficient training.

So the alternative has been absorbed rather than adopted. So the alternative has been absorbed rather than adopted: where state-space models reach production at all they are mostly hybrids, interleaving a small number of attention layers among many recurrent ones to buy constant-cost bulk memory while retaining some exact recall — though the frontier long-context systems remain pure attention stacks. Mamba-2 then showed the two families to be views of one class of structured sequence transformations, which makes the rivalry look less like a fork than a spectrum with two named endpoints.

transformer>s4.lead: S4 is the alternative answer to a question the Transformer had made central by 2020: how does a sequence model connect events tens of thousands of steps apart? Attention answers by enumeration — score every pair and let the data decide. S4 answers with a prior, a linear dynamical system whose state is provably a good running summary of its own history, and gets long range from theory rather than from brute force.

blocks.b:
By making one-hop access between arbitrary positions the standard, the Transformer turned long-range modelling from an architecture question into a cost question, and the efficient-attention literature that followed attacked the cost. Long Range Arena was assembled in 2020 to arbitrate between those variants, and its hardest task, Path-X, asks whether two dots in a sixteen-thousand-step flattened image are joined by a path. **Every attention variant tested sat at chance.**

That result is the precondition for S4. It established, on a benchmark the attention community had designed for itself, that making an all-pairs matrix cheaper is not the same as making it reach further, and that the failure might lie in the approach rather than in the budget.

S4 keeps the Transformer's containing architecture — a stack of identical residual blocks alternating a sequence mixer with a position-wise MLP — and replaces only the mixer. In place of data-dependent weights it uses a fixed linear recurrence, and it exploits the fact that a fixed recurrence is a convolution, computable across the whole sequence at once rather than unrolled.

Two additions make the removal survivable. HiPPO initialisation gives a state that approximates its own history under an explicit measure instead of decaying arbitrarily, and the normal-plus-low-rank parameterisation makes the convolution kernel computable in near-linear time — the engineering that turned a known idea into a working model. It also gains a mode attention has no analogue for: the same weights can be run as a recurrence at inference, constant memory per step, nothing cached.

S4 took Path-X well above chance and set the standard on raw audio and long time series, where the signal is long, dense and smooth — the regime attention handles worst. It opened a line of work rather than delivering a product: DSS and S4D soon showed a diagonal state matrix suffices, removing most of the algebraic difficulty, and H3 and then Mamba addressed what S4 could not do at all.

The cost is content-blindness. A time-invariant kernel treats every token identically, so the model cannot choose to look at one thing rather than another, and on language — where the useful primitives are copying, matching and retrieval — S4 lagged Transformers badly at equal compute. The alternative path did not replace attention; it identified a competence attention lacked, and needed two more years of work before it could compete on text.

bert>albert.lead: ALBERT keeps BERT's encoder and its masked-language-model pretraining almost unchanged, and attacks one number: the parameter count. What travelled was the whole recipe. What was thrown out was the assumption that every layer needs weights of its own.

blocks.b:
BERT's transferable result was that capacity in the encoder pays: BERT-large, at 24 layers and roughly 340M parameters, beat BERT-base at 12 layers and 110M on GLUE and SQuAD. That made width and depth the obvious lever, and immediately made them the obvious problem — the next step up did not fit comfortably in accelerator memory, and the weights have to be synchronised across every data-parallel worker at every step.

Two structural facts of the design were what ALBERT could exploit. The input embedding matrix is $V \times H$ over a WordPiece vocabulary of about 30k, so widening the hidden size $H$ drags a vocabulary-sized matrix along with it. And every layer carries its own attention and feed-forward weights, even though they are all trained to operate on the same residual stream and do broadly similar work.

ALBERT factorises the embedding. Instead of projecting one-hot tokens straight into $H$ dimensions it passes through a small $E$-dimensional space, $V \times E$ then $E \times H$, with $E \ll H$. The justification is a real distinction: WordPiece embeddings are context-independent and hidden states are context-dependent, so there is no reason the two should share a width. Second, all parameters are shared across layers, attention and feed-forward alike, so depth becomes free in storage.

What had to be added is the width the savings bought — ALBERT-xxlarge runs $H = 4096$ and still comes in under BERT-large. The pretraining objective changed too: next-sentence prediction was replaced by sentence-order prediction, which asks whether two consecutive segments have been swapped. NSP drew its negatives from other documents and could be solved on topic alone; SOP cannot be.

ALBERT-xxlarge took the state of the art on GLUE, SQuAD and RACE with fewer parameters than BERT-large, which was read as evidence that BERT had been badly over-parameterised. The reading was half right. Sharing weights reduces what you store and what you synchronise; it does nothing to the multiply-accumulates, and ALBERT-xxlarge, being much wider, is slower per token than the model it beat. The eighteen-fold figure belongs to ALBERT-large against BERT-large, a configuration that is also about 1.7x faster to train; it is ALBERT-xxlarge, the model that took the state of the art, whose parameter count and wall-clock cost point in opposite directions — fewer weights stored, roughly three times slower per step.

The durable lesson is that storage and inference cost are separate axes, and that conflating them misleads. Aggressive cross-layer sharing did not survive into later encoders. The finding about NSP did travel, though RoBERTa arrived at the same place more bluntly, by deleting the sentence-level objective altogether.

bert>distilbert.lead: DistilBERT changes neither the objective family nor the shape of the encoder. It changes who supplies the target: a trained BERT's full softmax over the vocabulary replaces the one-hot masked token, and that richer signal is what makes deleting half the layers survivable.

blocks.b:
Once BERT is pretrained it is a fixed function, and its output at a masked position is a distribution over some 30,000 WordPieces rather than a single answer. The mass it puts on the wrong tokens encodes which of them were plausible — a similarity structure over the vocabulary that a one-hot label does not contain. Hinton's distillation argument is that this is the useful part of a large model's behaviour, and that a small model can be fitted to it far more sample-efficiently than to hard labels.

The second thing BERT supplied was redundancy. Probing work had found adjacent layers computing closely related things, which suggested depth could be cut without cutting width — and, more usefully, that a student half as deep could be initialised from every other teacher layer rather than from scratch.

The student is BERT-base with every second layer deleted: six layers, the same hidden width, initialised from the teacher's surviving layers. Token-type embeddings and the pooler go, and so does next-sentence prediction.

The removal is paid for by a three-part loss. A distillation term matches the student's softened output to the teacher's, both taken at temperature $T$ with $p_i = \exp(z_i/T)/\sum_j \exp(z_j/T)$, which flattens the distribution so the small probabilities carry gradient. The ordinary masked-language-model term keeps the student anchored to real data, not only to the teacher's errors. A cosine term aligns the direction of student and teacher hidden states, so the residual stream stays in the teacher's geometry instead of finding its own. The result is a model 40% smaller and around 60% faster that retains roughly 97% of BERT's GLUE score.

This edge made distillation the default route to a deployable encoder, and the specific pattern — copy alternate layers, then fit to the teacher — was refined at once by TinyBERT and MobileBERT, which distil attention maps and intermediate states as well as logits.

The cost is arithmetic the headline numbers hide. You cannot distil a teacher you have not trained, so total compute goes up; what you are buying is inference cost with training cost, which pays only when the model is served often enough. The retained 97% is an average over GLUE, and the shortfall is not spread evenly — it concentrates on the tasks that need multi-step inference rather than lexical matching. The student also inherits whatever the teacher got wrong, including its biases, without inheriting its calibration.

bert>electra.lead: BERT runs a full forward pass over every token and collects a learning signal from the 15% it masked. ELECTRA leaves the encoder and the fine-tuning protocol alone and replaces the objective with one that scores every position — which is where its compute efficiency comes from.

blocks.b:
BERT's masking rate is a compromise forced by the objective. Mask more and the context that has to support the reconstruction is destroyed; mask less and an already thin signal gets thinner. Either way the model pays for a full forward and backward pass over $n$ tokens and is trained at roughly $0.15n$ of them.

The objective has a second defect that BERT itself named. The `[MASK]` token appears in pretraining and never in fine-tuning, so the input distribution shifts between the two phases; the 80/10/10 mixture of mask, random and unchanged tokens is a partial patch on exactly this. Both faults belong to reconstruction as a task, not to the encoder, which is why they could be fixed without touching the architecture.

ELECTRA trains two networks. A small generator is an ordinary masked language model; it fills the masked positions by sampling from its own distribution. The discriminator — the model you keep — then classifies each position as original or replaced. The loss is binary and applies at all $n$ positions, so one pass over the sequence teaches the model everywhere.

What had to be added is the generator, together with the constraint that it stay weak: at roughly a quarter to a half the discriminator's size the task is hard but learnable, while a generator as strong as the discriminator makes it hopeless. Sampling severs the gradient path between the two, so this is not adversarial training — the generator is trained by ordinary maximum likelihood and thrown away afterwards. The discriminator never sees a `[MASK]`, so the pretrain/fine-tune mismatch goes with it.

blocks.h: What the bit per token cost
blocks.b:
The efficiency claim is the paper's point: ELECTRA reaches GLUE scores comparable to RoBERTa's for a fraction of the pretraining compute, and ELECTRA-small is trainable on a single GPU while beating a much larger GPT on the same benchmark. DeBERTaV3 later adopted the objective wholesale, keeping disentangled attention and swapping masked-language modelling for replaced-token detection.

The cost is that a discriminator is not a language model. An MLM head gives a distribution over the vocabulary at every position, which supports infilling, pseudo-perplexity scoring and candidate reranking; replaced-token detection yields one bit per position and none of that. There is also a second network to size and tune: the authors found tying the generator's and discriminator's input embeddings measurably better than leaving them separate, and the two losses need weighting against each other.

bert>deberta.lead: BERT adds a position embedding to a token embedding before the first layer, so every attention score afterwards is computed on a vector in which content and position are already mixed. DeBERTa keeps them as two vectors and lets the score decompose into the terms that relate them.

blocks.b:
BERT's positional scheme is a learnt absolute embedding added to the token embedding, and everything downstream operates on that sum. The dot product deciding whether position $i$ should attend to position $j$ therefore answers one blended question when there are really two: how compatible are these words, and how compatible are these places. A model can learn to separate them inside the projections, but nothing in the parameterisation helps it.

By 2020 the groundwork was laid. Shaw and colleagues had shown that injecting relative position directly into the attention score works better than adding absolute position at the input, and Transformer-XL had made relative encodings load-bearing rather than optional. DeBERTa's move was to take that seriously enough to carry a separate position vector through the entire stack instead of folding it in once.

Each token gets a content vector $H_i$ and a relative-position vector $P_{i|j}$, and the attention score becomes a sum of three cross terms — content-to-content, content-to-position and position-to-content:

$$A_{ij} = H_i W_q (H_j W_k)^\top + H_i W_q (P_{j|i} W_{k,r})^\top + P_{i|j} W_{q,r} (H_j W_k)^\top$$

The fourth possible term, position-to-position, is dropped: under a relative encoding it carries no information about the pair.

Going purely relative loses something real, and DeBERTa has to put it back. The paper's example is a sentence in which two nouns sit in near-identical local contexts and are told apart mainly by where they fall in the clause. The enhanced mask decoder therefore injects absolute positions late, just before the output softmax, so absolute information is available for prediction without being entangled with content in every layer.

blocks.h: The best encoder, at a price
blocks.b:
DeBERTa-large matched or beat RoBERTa-large while training on far less data, and a 1.5B-parameter version was the submission that first pushed a SuperGLUE score past the human baseline. DeBERTaV3 then combined this attention with ELECTRA's replaced-token detection, and the result is still a common default wherever a discriminative encoder is wanted: classification, reranking, reward models over text.

The direct cost is attention arithmetic — three score terms rather than one, plus projections for the position stream, a real if modest overhead per layer. The larger cost is historical. This refines an architecture the field was in the process of leaving, and the insight it embodies, that position belongs in the attention score rather than added to the input, reached generative models by another route: rotary embeddings, which achieve the same separation with no extra parameters at all.

bert>t5.lead: This is a fork rather than a descent. T5 and BART take BERT's corrupt-and-reconstruct pretraining and put it on an encoder-decoder that can emit arbitrary text, which removes the need for a task-specific head and, with it, BERT's central limitation.

blocks.b:
BERT's transferable finding was not the `[CLS]` token or next-sentence prediction but denoising itself: corrupt an input, train a deep bidirectional model to restore it, and the representations that fall out transfer almost everywhere. That result is about the objective, not the architecture, which is why it could be lifted onto a different model shape.

The limitation is structural. An encoder emits one vector per input token, so any task whose output is not a label or a span over the input needs machinery bolted on top. Summarisation, translation and open-ended question answering need a decoder BERT does not have. The masking patch also left a pretrain/fine-tune mismatch that no amount of head engineering could reach, because the mismatch lives in the input.

BART keeps a full sequence-to-sequence transformer and corrupts the input however is convenient — token masking, deletion, sentence permutation, and text infilling, where a span of unknown length is replaced by a single mask so the model must decide how much is missing. Infilling mattered most. T5 narrows this to span corruption and makes the target cheap: dropped spans become numbered sentinel tokens and the decoder emits only the missing spans, not the whole sequence.

What had to be added is the decoder — roughly a second stack plus cross-attention — and a convention: every task is text in, text out, with a prefix such as `translate English to German:` selecting the behaviour. The classification and span-extraction heads go. T5 added an ablation grid on C4, comparing architectures, objectives and corruption rates that had previously been compared only across papers.

The text-to-text convention is what made multi-task fine-tuning expressible at all; T0 and later FLAN-T5 are T5 checkpoints — the original FLAN instruction-tuned a decoder-only model — and the habit of writing the task into the input as natural language passed from here into decoder-only models, where it became prompting. BERT's line did not die either — encoders remain right for retrieval and reranking, where you want a vector rather than a sample.

The encoder-decoder pays twice. Every inference runs both stacks and the cross-attention, and producing a class label as generated text is slower and looser than reading a softmax, since nothing constrains the output to be a valid label. At scale, decoder-only won for a simpler reason: it needs no decision about where to split the input, and every token yields a prediction. What survives of T5 is the framing, and its encoder as the text tower of image generators.

transformer>txl.lead: A Transformer language model carries no state between forward passes, so a corpus must be cut into fixed-length segments trained in isolation. Transformer-XL caches the previous segment's hidden states and attends into them — and that one change forces absolute positional encodings out.

blocks.b:
Self-attention gives a one-step path between any two positions inside its window and no path at all outside it. The character-level Transformer language models that preceded Transformer-XL fixed a segment length $L$ of a few hundred tokens, and no dependency longer than $L$ could be represented — not because the attention was too weak, but because the two tokens were never in the same forward pass.

That costs twice. Context fragmentation means the first tokens of every segment are predicted with almost no context at all. And at evaluation the only way to give each prediction a full window is to slide the segment forward one token and recompute everything, so the cost per predicted token is a whole forward pass over $L$ tokens.

Transformer-XL keeps the hidden states of segment $\tau$ and concatenates them, under a stop-gradient, to the states of segment $\tau+1$ at every layer. Queries come only from the current segment; keys and values come from both. Because each layer's cache was itself computed with a cache beneath it, the effective context grows with depth instead of staying at $L$.

The cache breaks absolute positions. If indices are assigned from the start of a segment, a cached key and a current key at the same offset carry identical encodings, and the model cannot tell which segment a key came from, exactly where the distinction matters most. So relative encodings had to be added: the query's absolute position term becomes two learnt global biases and the key's position enters as a sinusoid of the offset $i-j$. This is a consequence of caching, not an independent improvement.

The paper reports attention spans around 450% longer than a vanilla Transformer's and evaluation up to roughly 1,800 times faster, since each segment's states are computed once and reused rather than recomputed under a sliding window, alongside state-of-the-art perplexity on enwik8, text8 and WikiText-103. The relative-position formulation had the longer life of the two ideas: it reappears as T5's bucketed bias and, in spirit, in rotary and ALiBi schemes.

The recurrence is cruder than it looks. The stop-gradient means the model never learns what to retain; it keeps everything for one segment and then discards by age, which is memory without a controller. The cache costs memory, segments must be processed in order within a stream, and the quadratic cost inside a segment is untouched. Transformer-XL moved the horizon rather than changing the complexity.

txl>xlnet.lead: XLNet is Transformer-XL's backbone under a different objective. The segment cache and the relative positions carry over essentially unchanged, while the left-to-right factorisation is replaced by an expectation over factorisation orders — which is how it obtains bidirectional context without ever showing the model a mask token.

blocks.b:
Two properties of the backbone were preconditions rather than conveniences. It is autoregressive, so it trains on real sequences: no `[MASK]` in the input, and no assumption that the predicted tokens are independent of one another given the context. That second point is BERT's subtler flaw — mask both halves of a name and predict them from the surrounding text, and the joint is factorised into independent terms, losing exactly the dependency worth learning.

And it uses relative positional encodings. Under a permuted factorisation the step index in the ordering is not the position in the sentence, so any scheme keyed to absolute order within a pass would become meaningless. Relative encodings, computed from true sequence positions, survive the reordering intact. XLNet reuses the segment cache simply because long context is free once the backbone provides it.

The objective maximises likelihood under a random ordering:

$$\max_\theta \; \mathbb{E}_{z \sim \mathcal{Z}_T} \left[ \sum_{t=1}^{T} \log p_\theta\!\left(x_{z_t} \mid x_{z_{<t}}\right) \right]$$

where $\mathcal{Z}_T$ is the set of permutations of the positions. The tokens themselves are not shuffled — only the order in which they are conditioned on, implemented by masking the attention matrix, so content and positional encodings stay in natural order.

This breaks the usual parameterisation. A hidden state summarising $x_{z_{<t}}$ knows nothing about which position it is being asked to predict, so two different targets would receive the same distribution. XLNet adds two-stream attention: a content stream that sees the token, and a query stream that sees the position being predicted but not its content. Only the final fraction of each permutation is predicted, since terms conditioned on almost nothing are hopeless and slow convergence badly.

blocks.h: The objective that did not survive
blocks.b:
XLNet beat BERT across a broad sweep of tasks on publication. Within months RoBERTa showed that most of the gap closed when BERT was trained on comparable data for comparable time with next-sentence prediction removed — XLNet had used a much larger corpus — which reframed the comparison as being about training budget at least as much as permutation.

What survived this edge is not the objective. Two-stream attention doubles the attention bookkeeping, partial prediction discards most of each pass, and convergence was slow enough to be hard to justify. What did survive is Transformer-XL's cache and relative positions, which became standard, and XLNet's diagnosis: mask mismatch and the independence assumption are genuine defects of masked-language modelling. ELECTRA answered the first more cheaply; decoder-only scaling answered the second by dropping bidirectional pretraining altogether.

gpt3>cot.lead: In-context learning turned the prompt into a programming surface: GPT-3 continues in whatever form its demonstrations take. Chain-of-thought prompting is the observation that if the demonstrations contain the working and not only the answer, the model produces working too — and that this changes which problems it can solve, with no gradient update anywhere.

blocks.b: GPT-3 established that a large enough model conditions on a handful of demonstrations and continues in kind, so specifying a task became a matter of arranging the context. But the demonstrations were pairs of input and output, which fixes the answer to arrive in one shot. A transformer applies a fixed depth of computation per token, and the only serial budget it has beyond that depth is the tokens it has already emitted; a problem needing many dependent steps has nowhere to put them. The symptom was a flat scaling curve: on GSM8K, the grade-school word problems of Cobbe et al., few-shot accuracy barely moved with model size while everything else did, and the remedy on offer was fine-tuning with a trained verifier over samples — supervision, per task.

Wei et al. replaced each demonstration pair with a triple: input, the reasoning that reaches the answer, then the answer. Eight hand-written exemplars, a frozen model, no fine-tuning and no new data. What is discarded is the assumption that the answer must come out of one forward pass; what has to be added to make the removal work is scale, because the chain is only as good as the model's unconditioned continuation. Below roughly 100B parameters the gains vanish and often reverse — smaller models emit fluent, locally plausible chains that are wrong, and the extra length compounds the error. Kojima et al. then showed much of the effect survives with no exemplars at all, from the bare instruction to think step by step — evidence that the ability was already latent and prompting only addressed it.

blocks.h: Compute you can buy at inference
blocks.b: With chain-of-thought prompting a 540B model passed the fine-tuned-with-verifier result on GSM8K. The structural consequence matters more: the number of tokens spent before answering became a compute dial available at inference, on a model already trained. Everything after treats it as one: self-consistency samples many chains and takes the majority answer, and o1 eventually trains the chain rather than prompting for it. Theory followed the practice, showing that intermediate tokens strictly increase what a fixed-depth transformer can compute. The costs: a longer, slower, dearer answer for every query; a gain confined to models past a scale threshold; and a chain that is not a record of the computation. Models will write a chain supporting an answer that was actually determined by a cue the chain never mentions.

cot>o1.lead: Chain-of-thought prompting can only summon reasoning that pretraining already left in the model; on a problem the base distribution never solves, no phrasing helps. o1 takes the chain out of the prompt and makes it the object of training, shaped by large-scale reinforcement learning whose reward OpenAI did not disclose, though the field has read it as keyed to whether the final answer is right.

blocks.b: Chain-of-thought established the two things o1 builds on: that intermediate tokens are where multi-step work can be done at all, and that their quantity is a dial worth turning. What it could not do is add anything. Prompting is conditional sampling from a distribution fixed at the end of pretraining, so if a correct chain has negligible probability under that distribution no prompt raises it, and the failure modes stay the base model's: an arithmetic slip carried forward unchecked, no revisiting of a decomposition that is not working. Two lines of work had already shown the chain was trainable material rather than a prompt format: STaR sampled chains, kept those that reached the known answer and fine-tuned on them; and Lightman et al. found a reward model scoring each step beat one scoring only the outcome.

blocks.h: Training the chain, not the answer
blocks.b: o1 is trained with large-scale reinforcement learning to produce a long chain of thought before it answers. The format from chain-of-thought is kept; what is thrown away is the idea that the chain is a byproduct of answering, since here it is the thing optimised, credited or blamed as a whole by a reward attached to the outcome. What had to be added is the behaviour prompting never reliably produced: noticing an error mid-chain and going back, abandoning a decomposition, spending unequal effort on the hard sub-step. OpenAI reported accuracy improving along two axes, training-time RL compute and test-time thinking length; the second is new, since a pretrained model's quality is fixed once its run ends. The raw chains are withheld from the user, deliberately left unconstrained so they can be monitored without training pressure to look presentable.

blocks.h: A second scaling axis, and the bill
blocks.b: The results reported are on exactly the problems where prompting had stalled: olympiad-qualifier mathematics, competitive programming, graduate-level science questions. That reframed the field's spending: capability stopped being bought only in the pretraining run and became something bought per query, which is why inference cost is now variable and reasoning is sold as a tier. Latency and price now rise with the thinking, unpredictably per question. The gains concentrate in domains where the answer can be checked, and o1 was not preferred over its predecessor on some open-ended writing tasks. And optimising a hidden intermediate against a terminal reward gives no reason for the trace to be a faithful account of how the answer was reached — it is now both unverified and unseen.

instructgpt>o1.lead: What travels along this arrow is the machinery, not the objective. InstructGPT established reinforcement learning on a pretrained language model as a distinct post-training stage, with a learned model of human preference at the reward end. o1 keeps the stage and replaces the reward with a check on whether the answer is correct.

blocks.b: The pipeline was not new — Ziegler et al., then Stiennon et al. on summarisation, had already fitted a reward model to human comparisons and optimised against it — but InstructGPT is what made it the standard finish for a general-purpose model: sampling completions from the policy, scoring them and updating by policy gradient. Every detail followed from the reward being a proxy. The score came from a network fitted to labeller comparisons, so a per-token KL penalty back to the supervised model kept the policy inside the region where those scores still tracked human judgement, and the RL was a light finishing pass rather than a serious share of the compute. The claim it demonstrated is the one o1 depends on: a 1.3B preference-tuned model was preferred to 175B GPT-3, so post-training against the right objective can buy more than an order of magnitude of pretraining. By 2024 that mattered more, as each added pretraining token returned less.

o1 keeps the shape of the stage and changes the judge. OpenAI has not described what scores the sample, but the reading the field acted on is that where a competition mathematics problem or code with tests can be checked, correctness is established without a human and without a learned model, so the signal is ground truth rather than an estimate of what a labeller would like. Three properties change with it. The reward does not decay as the policy moves away from its initialisation, so the leash can be loosened and RL can become the training run instead of a polish. It does not saturate at the resolution of human comparison, so it can absorb far more compute. And it lands on a hidden intermediate that no one ranks, so credit must be assigned across a long trace from one terminal signal, rather than to the one visible response a labeller read.

Post-training splits in two, and both halves stay. Preference tuning remains, because correctness cannot say whether an answer is helpful, safe or decently phrased, and verifier-based RL is stacked on top wherever a checker exists; the reasoning models since do both. The cost is coverage. Checkers exist for arithmetic and unit tests, not for an essay, a diagnosis or advice, so capability grows lopsidedly, strongest exactly where scoring is easy — which is not where most of the work is. And a checker is still a proxy. Reward hacking migrates from flattering the reward model to satisfying the test: reaching the right string by an unintended route, or special-casing the input. The failure mode is relocated rather than removed, and it is harder to catch once the trace is hidden.

o1>r1.lead: o1 shipped a result and withheld the method: hidden chains, no paper, and the training described only in outline. R1's contribution is to show that the essential part reproduces from a published recipe on open weights, and that the piece which looked hardest — the deliberation itself — needs no supervised traces at all.

blocks.h: An existence proof, not a method
blocks.b: o1 made public two facts the field could act on without knowing how they were obtained: that reinforcement learning over long chains yields a qualitatively different problem-solver, and that accuracy keeps rising as the chain runs longer at inference. That is enough to justify the expense of attempting it, and not enough to attempt it any particular way. The obvious readings were the expensive ones — a process reward model grading every step, or tree search over partial chains. DeepSeek report trying both and abandoning them: the step-level reward model was gamed by the policy and had to be retrained continually, and search needed a token-level action space and a value model that would not train well. What survived was the cheapest hypothesis, that rewarding only the final answer might be sufficient.

blocks.h: Pure RL on a base model
blocks.b: R1-Zero applies GRPO to DeepSeek-V3-Base with no supervised fine-tuning first and no reasoning traces to imitate. The reward is two rules: does the extracted answer match, and is the reasoning inside the required tags. Nothing rewards length, self-checking or backtracking; those emerge anyway, with average response length climbing steadily over training as the model starts revisiting its own steps and dropping approaches mid-solution. AIME 2024 pass@1 goes from 15.6% to 71.0%. The removal costs legibility — with nothing in the reward attending to it, the chains mix languages and are hard to read — so R1 proper adds back a small cold-start fine-tune on curated long chains, a language-consistency term in the reward, and a final preference stage, buying readability at some cost in raw score.

The weights are released under a permissive licence and the recipe is written down, so the capability stops being one laboratory's. The accompanying distillation result sharpens the point: fine-tuning Qwen and Llama models on chains generated by R1 beat running the same reinforcement learning on those small models directly. The search is the expensive part, and once any model has done it the result transfers by imitation. That is also the cost. Visible chains are distillable chains, so publishing them shortens whatever lead they represent and pushes the incentive back towards hiding them. Rule-based rewards confine the training to domains with a checker, which leaves the same lopsidedness o1 has. And the failure modes are reported rather than concealed: language mixing, sensitivity to prompt phrasing — few-shot prompting makes it worse — and the reward hacking that made them rule out a learned reward model in the first place.
